proposed_updates.paper_title: ML-driven strategies for adapting immunotherapy in metastatic NSCLC

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper uses methodology that has been developed by others and is readily available for use in a convenient R package, 'personalized'; the contribution of this paper is the application of said methodology to personalization of cancer treatments. There is nothing wrong with that, but the author occasionally use language that obscures this important fact. For instance, the statements 'the study introduces an innovative approach' or 'this methodological framework aims to revolutionize treatment selection' in the abstract can be easily misunderstood.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the comment, revised abstract language, and introduced an A-STEP ensemble framework as additional novel methodological contribution.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The CI methods are based on some important assumptions such as: no residual confounding, SUTVA, etc. These assumptions are not stated or discussed anywhere in the manuscript as far as I can tell, which would be important to do because they may not always be reasonable in practice.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Supplementary Methods S2 explicitly stating no-residual-confounding, SUTVA, and treatment-ignorability assumptions and discussed their plausibility in practice.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of the word 'validation' in this study is problematic. The methodology hinges on estimating individual/group-specific treatment effects (ITE), which is only possible under strong assumptions. The 'validation' performed in this paper consists of estimating ITEs in a different dataset and then showing, essentially, that ITEs are higher for people who actually received the recommended treatment. However this doesn't 'validate' the model in the sense that the assumptions used to construct it are not checked. A more direct validation would need to use randomized data (could be retrospective), and would need to show that the actual treatment outcomes of patients who received the recommended treatments were better than those who did not.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added two external validation cohorts (Dana-Farber n=1077, Stand Up To Cancer n=393) and reported weighted risk-reduction (Table 3) plus Kaplan-Meier survival curves with hazard ratios, demonstrating better outcomes in patients who received model-recommended therapy.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To the extent that validation was performed, there seems to be no check whether the 'treatment effects conditional on subgroups' are statistically significant. It seems like the 'personalized' package does provide methods to perform such tests. Additionally, correction for multiple testing could be needed given that 5 different loss functions were tried.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed FDR multiple-testing correction in revision; reviewer noted in Round 2 that only 1 of 8 tested models remained significant under correction, and questioned use of FDR 0.1 instead of Bonferroni.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: All five methods that were proposed in the original version of this manuscript failed to work in the two validation cohorts. I am afraid this was the reason why three new methods (H-STEP, S-STEP, and A-STEP) were also added, although that is not made clear. Of these three new methods, only A-STEP can be 'validated' in the two new cohorts; however, the p-values for the two arms are 0.016 and 0.0076. Since the authors have now tried 8 methods in total on this data, some kind of p-value correction should be applied to correct for this fact. So, in total, it could be questionable that the new proposed A-STAR method—which seems to have been developed using the validation data more than once—would actually generalize.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed FDR p-value correction but reviewer remained dissatisfied in subsequent round, noting that the corrected significance bar (FDR 0.1) is lenient and that the A-STEP method appears to have been developed using the validation set.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The methods are tested by determining the survival in the cohorts of those patients who receive the treatment recommended by the model to those who were not treated as recommended by the model. As remarked in the previous manuscript, direct validation of this kind of method would require analysis of a randomized rather than observational trial. While the authors do employ propensity score matching in an attempt to reduce confounding, we still need to buy that there is no residual confounding, which can be questionable since some important clinical variables seem to be missing (see comment by R4). Unfortunately, this point was not really addressed by the revision.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion of residual confounding limitation but did not perform randomized validation; reviewer noted point remained inadequately addressed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Their study hinges on their ability to identify and control for bias arising from intrinsic differences between patients selected for ICI-mono and ICI-chemo—the reviewer is not convinced that with their limited clinical data, that does not for example include Performance Status, they would be able to do this meaningfully. There is no description of how the genomic mutation markers were derived, or what they were, anywhere in the paper.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added clinical-variable list, expanded cohort to multiple centers, and clarified mutation feature derivation, but did not include Performance Status (likely unavailable in source data).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors choose to identify 3-months progression as a binary endpoint. I wonder why this choice was made rather than using the full survival data, since the R package 'personalized' supports time-to-event outcomes.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added progression-free-survival analyses (Kaplan-Meier with HRs) alongside binary 3-month endpoint in the revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors stated that they will only make the code available upon publication (p. 25) so I was unable to review the code.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors made code publicly available at https://github.com/WuLabMDA/A-STEP with documentation for replicating results.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: An issue for this reader with respect to the field of personalized medicine in general is the use of terminology, such as 'personalized immunotherapy' or the expression of an objective to seek 'optimal personalized treatment strategies' implying that the outcome of this work will be the identification of the optimal treatment for an individual. In fact, the process of determining the best treatment allocation can be viewed as a task of subgroup identification.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors softened language and clarified in Round 2 that the analysis is subgroup identification, and revised abstract/introduction tone in Round 3.

reviewer_strengths.text: A data driven and rigorous approach for this purpose. The use of multi-center data and the addition of external testing cohorts is notable.
I commend the authors for applying sound causal inference methodology in this field. These methods could be interesting for the development of personalized medicine.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Three review rounds. Reviewer #2 escalated concerns about post-hoc method addition (A-STEP developed after original 5 methods failed on validation cohorts) — this is a strong test-set-reuse / model-selection-leakage signal that remained partially unresolved. Reviewer #4 recommended rejection in Round 1 citing data opacity and lack of code.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Precision phenotyping of type 2 diabetes in chinese populations using a variational autoencoder-informed tree model

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The description of the study population is not sufficient. It is described that included individuals are those with T2D within 12 months prior to baseline, where baseline is the first recorded instance of T2D in the database. This makes no sense, as that would imply no T2D events prior to baseline.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that 'newly diagnosed T2D' (≤12 months) was the inclusion criterion using first-ever ICD-10 E11 record cross-checked against medical notes and prescriptions to confirm diagnosis date.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a lack of justification as to why individuals with major medical conditions were excluded (exclusion criteria (d)).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors justified exclusion of patients with malignancy, organ transplantation, ESRD to reduce confounding from intensive treatments and comorbidities; reviewer noted this also limits real-world applicability since ~33% of diabetes patients are multimorbid.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Outlier removal and rank normalization is performed without an explicit why (important!) and how (i.e. how was rank normalization in practice performed) and most importantly how many records it affects, and how it e.g. affects the results if it is not considered (as a sensitivity analysis). Adding complex data-preprocessing steps greatly increases model pipeline complexity so these choices should be justified.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors provided detailed justification (values >5 SD removed, n=575 outliers tabled by variable), explained that rank normalization ensures non-zero variance for DDRTree PCA step, and added sensitivity analysis to supplements.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a lack of detail in the description of the methods to a point where reproducing the experiments are impossible. The number of cross validation folds is not specified, and libraries of the machine learning algorithms considered are not specified, nor definitions of their hyperparameter spaces.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors expanded Methods section with details on 10-fold CV, hyperparameter search spaces, and library versions in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is claimed that the GBC method achieves 'highest accuracy' and therefore is chosen as a 'final model'. However, the authors are considering a multitude of outcomes so is that really the case for ALL of these? In addition, is accuracy really the best measure to consider? One could imagine that some of the considered outcomes are rare leading to class imbalance. Alternative measures not so sensible to class imbalance (e.g. ROC or PR AUC) should at the very least be considered for model selection, and at the very least reported. Further – there is no mention of how the prediction threshold was decided.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added ROC AUC and PR AUC for all models in revision; reviewer still flagged that hyperparameter selection process remained unclear.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Code availability: Given the lack of detail in the description of the methods and no code availability it is impossible to reproduce the presented results of the manuscript, even if one would have access to the data.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors expanded methods documentation; code availability not fully resolved in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It remains unclear whether the VAE is used for representation learning, feature selection, denoising, or all three, and why this choice is preferable to simpler alternatives (e.g. a vanilla autoencoder, PCA, or purely supervised selection). Assertions about 'informative' latent structure and 'denoised input' are not supported by comparative analyses.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified VAE role as feature ranking/selection and added LASSO/elastic-net comparison, but reviewer noted that implementation details (full-set vs subset, hyperparameter tuning, nested CV) remained ambiguous.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The manuscript lacks essential details on hyperparameter search spaces, selection criteria, and safeguards against data leakage. Model performance is reported without clear nested CV, fold definitions. It is also unclear when models use the full feature set versus the 10 'VAE-selected' features.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added clarifications but reviewer indicated several questions remained unanswered.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The proposed 'stability' metric based on cosine similarity across independently trained VAEs is not valid given rotational/permutation of latent spaces.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully resolved in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The inclusion of non-diabetic controls in representation learning is not sufficiently justified if the stated goal is to extract diabetes-specific patterns. The chosen case:control ratio is also not motivated. On the other hand, exclusion of multimorbid individuals may limit real-world applicability and should be addressed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors stated controls were included to enhance contrast for diabetes-specific phenotyping; reviewer remained unconvinced.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Statements about longitudinal 'phenotypic shift,' superiority of DDRTree over traditional clustering, mitigation of confounding via VAE-based selection, clinical relevance of the continuous model, and 'early interventions' are insufficiently supported by statistical testing, benchmarking, or appropriate references.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully resolved in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The observation was that HbA1c had modest effect, while lipids had the most substantial effect. This is surprising, as one would expect HbA1c to be the strongest driver when studying diabetes outcomes. Also, liver disease exerts an undue influence on specific phenotypes such as DR and CVD. The authors must consider reporting the burden of liver diseases in the sample for each diabetes complication explored in this manuscript as a table.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully described in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: BMI differences between ethnicities could introduce specific errors, especially in cases like this, where there is evidence of interplay of BMI with other risk factors. Does this also imply that the effect of BMI on diabetes phenotypes may have been masked due to the mismatch?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully described in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: 'The data included all the patients whose data is accessible from the participating centers' medical record systems.' Were all the data during the period accessible in those centers? If not, what are the percentages of accessible data, and what determined the accessibility? In addition, it is good to know the distribution of these 24 medical centers.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully described in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The rationale for selecting exactly ten features in the final model is not clearly explained. Why was this number chosen? It would be helpful if the authors could clarify whether they tested different numbers of input features and how this affected the tree structure, complication risk gradients, or model performance.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully described in extracted pages.

reviewer_strengths.text: The study leverages a massive electronic health record dataset, robust statistical models, and external validations across independent cohorts, significantly enhancing the credibility and generalizability of the findings.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Three rounds. Reviewer #1 was unusually thorough — 15 initial comments expanded to 45 in Round 2 with significant remaining methodological gaps (data leakage safeguards, nested CV, VAE justification). Many Round-2 concerns ended without clear final resolution (Reviewer #1 was satisfied with typos only by Round 3). Reviewers #2 and #3 accepted earlier.

proposed_updates.paper_title: AMR-GNN: a multi-representation graph neural network framework to enable genomic antimicrobial resistance prediction

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Lines 117-118: broth microdilution and agar dilution are very different approaches? The same isolate could have different AMR phenotypes using these two different models. How do you think this will impact the model?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors noted CLSI permits both methods for P. aeruginosa AST, applied agar-dilution data to four antimicrobials with AUROCs 0.869–0.977, and argued expansion of training data enhanced rather than compromised performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Line 123-126: I don't really understand why you selected the external validation data from two small datasets rather than pooling the data and randomly selecting the data. This could have avoided some of the phenotype imbalances.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that pooling/random selection was already performed for the internal test set; the two smallest datasets were reserved as a true hold-out set to assess generalisability while maximising training data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Some of the datasets are quite imbalanced, which could cause issues with overfitting.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added class-specific weights to binary cross-entropy loss to address imbalance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Lines 308-309: Do you think this drop in prediction accuracy could be due to the models being overfit, or that they did not have all the data required to train a model for better predictions?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors attributed the performance drop on hold-out to geographic specificity of AMR mechanisms (regional variants), noting ARDaP's comprehensive globally-curated database outperformed AMR-GNN in 3/6 external comparisons, and updated discussion to highlight need for continuous data integration.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Many of the tools do not have version numbers, which are necessary for reproducibility. The GitHub for AMR-GNN lacks information about what the model uses to predict and what outputs are expected. The output files do not have enough information for someone not familiar with neural networks. The GitHub should explain in detail what kind of input is expected and how the user can prepare their data to be in the correct format.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added version numbers, implemented Docker containerization and Snakemake workflow, updated output format to include binary AMR phenotype predictions, and added documentation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Benchmarks on other bacterial pathogens: it is impossible to assess the robustness of AMR-GNN performance without reference points (i.e., results obtained from other tools). I would kindly ask the authors to run VAMPr or ARIBA, or any AMR phenotype prediction tool, on these four datasets.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages; reviewer #2 accepted manuscript in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How do the authors know that ST is the optimal distance level to remove population effects? Also, how do the authors know that ST is the optimal distance level to control for clonal-structure bias?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The study employs performance metrics such as F1, AUROC, sensitivity, and specificity, [but] it overlooks what is arguably the most clinically critical metric in AMR prediction: the very major error (VME) rate. In addition, the reported F1 scores (Figure 3) are approximately 0.8, which is lower than those achieved by prior studies (e.g., F1 values around 0.92 were reported). As a result, it is not entirely clear whether this GNN-based approach offers superior performance compared to existing methods.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added VME rates to internal and external test set comparisons; AMR-GNN achieved superior VME in 5/5 internal and 4/6 external comparisons.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although the figures illustrate that the features are mainly derived from unitigs, SNPs, and FCGR, the description in the Methods section and the demo dataset provided suggest that AMR prediction does not directly start from genomic assemblies, but rather requires an adjacency matrix as input. The documentation provided on the website does not include instructions on how to train the AMR-GNN model or how to use genomic sequencing data to perform AMR prediction.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Snakemake workflow to generate input data from genome assemblies and Docker containerization; Reviewer #3 maintained that Docker-incompatible HPC environments still face usability barriers.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Content of the discussion section: while I found the overall manuscript very interesting, I'm afraid the Discussion section was particularly poor. The first five paragraphs consist of a long, and perhaps unnecessary, recapitulation of the results. There is no real discussion of the analyses. I would have liked some discussion of, for instance, the contribution of each feature type to performance, given their different nature, and which additional ones could be added in the future.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_strengths.text: The manuscript is well written, the figures are of top quality, and the supplementary files contain all required information (MIC values and sequence accession IDs). I particularly appreciated the stepwise testing of the algorithm in this study (single features vs full algorithm, with and without decoupling), which makes it clear how each component contributes to overall performance.
Strong performance lift from baseline (>28% increase for cefepime when using AMR-GNN); models extended to both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Genomic AMR is at the edge of MLGG scope (genomic features), but the prediction task is binary phenotype classification with clear cohort/split/external-validation concerns that map cleanly to MLGG gates. Two review rounds; Reviewer #3 remained partially dissatisfied with Docker dependency in code release.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Graph augmented transformers improve chemotherapy toxicity symptom extraction from clinical notes

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The methods state that patients with 'blood cancers' were excluded, but the results note that hematopoietic tumors were the most prevalent cancer type and discuss lymphoma patients. The authors should clarify the hematologic malignancies permitted in the study.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that only leukemia patients were excluded per OP-35 specifications; lymphoma and multiple myeloma were retained. Methods updated to state this explicitly.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is limited representation in the patient sample from certain patient races, and some cancer types are missing altogether (multiple myeloma, acute leukemia), which also can limit generalizability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged limitation in discussion, emphasized need for future validation across more diverse populations and cancer types.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The manuscript also claimed this is a 'retrospective cohort study', which is a specific study method in traditional epidemiology. This is not accurate, the study is more like a methodology development.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised terminology to 'methodology development and a validation study using retrospective EHR data' throughout the manuscript.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It's not clear how the evaluation was done. Is it evaluated based on span match, exact match or flexible match? There is an inconsistency in evaluation metrics AUROC and F1 were used in various instances, why? Reporting of results need more details, for example, what's the percentage of … 'Specifically, they detected 7 patients with Pain, 1 with Anemia, 4 with symptoms 313 related to DVND, and 4 with diagnoses linked to NPFS.' What's the impact of the percentage?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that flexible match was used (model must detect at least one mention corresponding to annotated symptom), reported weighted AUROC, AUPRC, precision, recall, F1 at threshold 0.5, plus Hamming Loss and subset metrics for multi-label setting.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The experiments are insufficient and some details are missing. For example, it is unknown if GAT-CN has an advantage over other graph-based methods or even rule-based approaches. It would be interesting to see the results with the 'term nodes' concatenated as a sequence rather than form a graph as the input.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Random Forest as rule-based-style baseline, included simple string-matching method using OP-35 Diagnosis Vocabulary, and argued that BioClinicalBERT (already in benchmark) serves as the sequence-based comparison; rule-based achieved 0.99 recall but 0.505 precision vs model's 0.780.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The current evaluation relies primarily on a single holdout test dataset. The absence of additional external or diverse datasets might limit insights into the generalizability of the GAT-CN model across various clinical settings or institutions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged limitation in discussion, citing single-cancer-center single-holdout design, and committed to multi-institutional validation as future work.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Currently, the model's performance analysis is primarily reported using the F1 metric. Including additional sensitivity analyses, such as precision-recall curves, ROC curves, or decision threshold analyses, would offer deeper insights and further contextualize the model's performance, particularly regarding its sensitivity and specificity trade-offs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added AUROC, AUPRC, precision, recall, F1 across symptom classes with PR and ROC curves.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: While the paper benchmarks the GAT-CN model against established transformer models, it should also include comparisons against newer state-of-the-art transformer models designed specifically for clinical text, such as Clinical-Longformer/BigBird and BioClinical ModernBERT.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained their reasoning in the revision; reviewer accepted in Round 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The supplementary materials lack detailed information regarding model training processes, specifically describing hyperparameter tuning procedures, parameter selection justifications, and including comprehensive training and evaluation loss curves. In the methods section, the manuscript does not describe the computational resources of deploying this model, including detailed metrics about training time, hardware requirements, resource utilization, and scalability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added computational resource information to Methods section.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The discussion did not address subgroup performance disparities, particularly regarding ethnicity, offering detailed hypotheses for observed disparities and proposing concrete, actionable strategies to improve model fairness, such as diversifying training data, targeted fine-tuning, or fairness-aware algorithmic adjustments.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added limitation acknowledging subgroup disparities risk and need for hybrid approaches to mitigate bias.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Results section, it is stated that the target cohort comprised 1753 patients who received acute care within 30 days of initiation of chemotherapy. However, in practical application for the proactive prediction of ACU events (as implied in the Introduction), the 30-day acute care status of patients would be necessarily unknown. If so, the applicability of the cohort to the intended task scenario might thus be further justified.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised terminology emphasizing the model performs symptom extraction temporally associated with toxicities rather than predictive ACU classification.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Model Evaluation subsection, it is stated that the ground truth for model performance evaluation was generated by manual annotation on patients' clinical notes (obtained before t_1, from Figure 2). However, if the intended objective is proactive prediction, the relevant ACUs would arise only after the notes were recorded (i.e. after t_1, before t_f). If so, it might be clarified as to whether the annotation using the clinical notes (obtained before t_1) would reflect future patient ACU (after t_1).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised manuscript to clarify model identifies symptoms temporally associated with chemotherapy-induced toxicities rather than performing causal prediction of future ACU.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Diagnosis Vocabulary and Note Annotation subsection, it is stated that the training and validation sets were labeled using patient OP-35 diagnosis codes in the EHR data, but the test set was manually annotated by four annotators. This difference in annotation between the training/validation and test sets might be explained - was annotation by diagnosis code inapplicable for the test set?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully extracted; authors revised methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Model Evaluation subsection, benchmarking against existing transformer-based models and baseline approaches was described. An ablation experiment with different embeddings as input to the graph model might be appropriate, to support the chosen Bio+ClinicalBERT embedding. For the Random Forest baseline approach, it might be clarified as to whether hyperparameter optimization had been attempted.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully extracted; authors added rule-based baseline.

reviewer_strengths.text: Dr. Saquand and colleagues demonstrate an innovative approach to the use of NLP for extracting symptoms and adverse event monitoring in patients with cancer. Overall, this is an excellent, timely and novel article.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Five reviewers. PR-EXP-0086 is NLP on clinical notes which is somewhat outside the traditional EHR-tabular MLGG scope, but the cohort/label/leakage concerns are directly mappable. Reviewer #6 raised the most methodologically important concern: temporal alignment between training labels (derived before t_1) and the claimed prospective ACU-prediction objective (events after t_1) — a classic future-information / target-leakage risk that was reframed rather than fully resolved.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Development and validation of prediction algorithm to identify tuberculosis in two large California health systems

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Generalisability beyond California is a potential concern, since only Californian data were used in development and validation. Do the authors see this as a tool for local use only, or do they envisage wider evaluation and implementation? If the latter, have they considered seeking external validation for example in Canada, where similar datasets exist?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified model is intended for California health systems only at present; noted validation in other geographic regions as important direction for future research and added 'in California' to abstract scope statement per Round 2 request.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It would be useful to know how well the Canadian model (which is intended for similar use) performs in the Californian data, as a benchmarking exercise.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors declined to benchmark, explaining the Canadian model targets recent immigrants (<5 years) while their model covers full health-system populations; key inputs (years in US, refugee status) are not available in their EHR, making head-to-head comparison infeasible.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The lack of calibration assessment is also a major concern. It is highly unusual not to report calibration performance, even for a rare outcome. This is certainly strongly recommended in TRIPOD reporting guidance and I would urge the authors to assess this formally.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added mean calibration and calibration slope to Results, Methods, Discussion, and Table 3.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The calibration assessment could still be improved. The authors present 'mean calibration'. By this, do they mean calibration in the large? If so, the usual ideal target value would be 0, rather than 1. This requires further explanation in the methods section, including how it was calculated and a citation. Alternatively, they could present observed:expected ratios instead of mean calibration. I also recommend adding calibration plots.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that mean calibration is exponentiated calibration-in-the-large (target value of 1), added McLernon et al. citation, and explained they avoided calibration plots due to extreme low-risk concentration in rare-disease distribution.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The abstract refers to the 'simulated' TB outcome, but not the observed TB outcome which I believe was also assessed?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors agreed in principle but cited 150-word abstract limit, kept simulated outcome only as most conservative summary; Results/Discussion/Conclusion cover both.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I did not see a link to the code. Apologies if I missed this.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors included code in resubmission along with simulated dataset to facilitate review.

reviewer_strengths.text: The use of the KPSC cohort for your training set and the external validation with the KPNC cohort elegantly provides similar cohorts, especially in regard to access to health insurance and access.

Overall, the analyses are reasonably well conducted and transparently reported. The effort to target LTBI testing is perfectly justifiable given that absolute risks of disease are very low among most populations.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Two rounds. Reviewer #1 mostly suggested wording/clarity edits (skipped as non-substantive). Reviewer #2 raised three substantive methodological points (generalisability, calibration, abstract reporting). Reviewer #3 was a co-reviewer (training role, no independent comments). Calibration concern is a clean example of MLGG-C01/E02 + TRIPOD-AI gap that was partially-but-incompletely resolved (Round-2 still flagged unclear calibration method).

proposed_updates.paper_title: Vision transformer-based model can optimize curative-intent treatment for patients with recurrent hepatocellular carcinoma

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is unclear how observer and internal technical variability regarding ultrasound (US) and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) were addressed in the study. Please provide detailed information on how variability among different observers and technical settings was managed. This could include standardization procedures, training protocols for observers, inter-observer reliability assessments, and calibration methods used to ensure consistency across examinations.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors detailed expertise of radiologists (10-20+ years), guideline-based acquisition protocols, multi-vendor equipment specifications, subgroup analyses showing no significant variability across centers/manufacturers, and three ablation studies.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is a discrepancy in the clinical settings between the development and validation sets, with the development set focusing on non-treated HCC and the validation set on recurrent HCC. Explain the rationale behind using different clinical settings for development and validation. Address how this difference might affect the model's performance and generalizability. Consider discussing any steps taken to mitigate potential biases introduced by this discrepancy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors collected additional rHCC data from two hospitals for the external testing cohort and performed subgroup analyses showing consistent performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A cohort from center A was included as an external validation set, but the patients were treated, and the scans were performed at the same center as the development cohort, which challenges the definition of 'external validation.' To ensure proper generalization testing, consider including results from only truly external centers (e.g., centers B and C).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added subgroup analyses across Centers A through E showing consistent C-index (0.72-0.76) and AUC.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper fails to compare its results with state-of-the-art (SOTA) Vision Transformer-based models that support multimodal data or publicly available datasets. Vision Transformers rely on the quality and diversity of the dataset because their performance is tied to the patterns they learn during training. Without testing on different publicly available datasets, it is difficult to establish the generalizability and robustness of the proposed approach. Moreover, the diversity of the training data is important for training Vision Transformers. Any bias in the training data, such as race or gender bias, can affect the model's predictions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed ablation studies including alternative DL models; SOTA ViT benchmarks on public datasets not added but multi-center Chinese cohorts emphasized.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Moreover, the comparisons with major guideline methods do not address inherent biases or limitations in the staging systems. This could undermine the validity of the results, as these biases can impact the model's performance. There is also a drop in performance metrics when the model is applied to the external testing cohort. This could indicate potential overfitting and limited generalizability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed subgroup analyses and ablation studies showing consistent performance; discussion expanded.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The study also does not provide detailed information on sex and gender considerations, failing to comply with the SAGER guidelines (as recommended in the review instructions).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added sex/age subgroup analyses in 2ndTA and 2ndSR datasets.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In addition, the statistical analysis lacks detailed justification for the selection of some specific tests and thresholds. The choice of propensity score matching (PSM) and the methods used to evaluate statistical significance are not sufficiently explained. The rationale behind the selection of specific variables and the chosen caliper value of 0.02 for PSM should be explicitly justified.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully extracted in available pages; authors expanded methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The actual goal of your study and the algorithm is not making a decision regarding which local therapy to use or if it should be used at all but to give an outlook on the prognosis of the patient, namely the OS/PFS. So the decision derived from this information would be to treat or not to treat locally – with the alternative being systemic treatment – or TACE/TARE (which we know to perform inferior to local ablation and surgery in suitable cases). Therefore the title is misleading. You do not investigate on how to improve HCC treatment. In order to give aid in the treatment decision, you would have to include patients in whom the therapy decision was wrong or suboptimal. But how do you know in your cohorts that the treatment they received was inferior to any other treatment option? You can't know that and neither your AI algorithm.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages; reviewer recommended title change to 'prognostication tool in HCC to be treated by means of local therapy'.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To include just T2w, DWI and CEUS sounds surprising. How did you decide to use these specific parts of the diagnostic work-up? What do you expect the AI to read on these images? We know that T2 signal and diffusion restriction loosely correlates with the grading of the tumors. What if you provided the algorithm with the grading of the tumors instead of MRI? Or to give just SI-values/radiomics from these images instead of letting the algorithm read this on its own? Or if you run the algorithm against sets of (para)clinical parameters, which are known to determine the prognosis and outcome of patients? As said previously, the clinical guideline based categories are not designed to give this fine granulated info on prognosis.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Training on initial hepatocellular carcinoma (iHCC) data for application to rHCC may introduce biases, despite biological similarities between the two. The geographic and demographic variability of datasets is noted but not deeply analyzed for potential biases.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not fully extracted in available pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: While the model architecture is described, details on hyperparameter optimization and model interpretability are limited. The explainability of the models is limited. Did the authors attempt to understand why the model classifies patients into low- or high-risk categories? Providing insights would enhance interpretability and clinical relevance.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Additionally, CEUS is rarely used as a surveillance tool in clinical practice, whereas CT is more commonly employed. This discrepancy should be addressed in the manuscript, as the lack of discussion on CT may limit the applicability of the study's findings.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_strengths.text: The paper uses a large multi-institutional dataset (8946 patients from three geographically distinct centers in China) and describes models for both thermal ablation and surgical patients, which is a strength.

The provided GitHub repository is well-documented. The README file offers an overview of the model's purpose, prerequisites, and instructions. Overall, the repository's organization and detailed documentation make it user-friendly and support the reproducibility of the paper's findings.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Paper uses vision transformer on multimodal imaging (US/CEUS/MRI) plus clinical variables. While imaging is at the boundary of MLGG scope (per project memo MLGG does not cover pure imaging), this study has substantive prediction-modeling concerns directly mappable to MLGG gates: dev-vs-validation cohort discrepancy (iHCC training, rHCC validation), same-center 'external' validation challenge, and Reviewer #4's title/causal-claim concern about prognostication being mis-framed as treatment optimization. Five reviewers, three rounds. Many Round-1 concerns from Reviewers #4 and #5 do not have clear Round-2 resolutions in extracted pages.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Personalized azithromycin treatment rules for children with watery diarrhea using machine learning

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Practical Applicability: While the authors demonstrate that risks of outcomes differ between groups, this alone does not prove the rule's practical utility. The lack of a test set, likely due to the limited number of cases, is a significant limitation of this approach.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added external dataset application section (Application to External Dataset) showing rules learned in ABCD data were applied to Global Enteric Multicenter Study (GEMS) data with similar treatment effect patterns (CCC 0.69 for comprehensive rule).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Performance Estimation: The use of 10-fold cross-validation yields performance metrics as averages across folds, which is not ideal for robust performance estimation. The authors should elaborate on the statistical basis for computing confidence intervals in this setting.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors cited Hubbard et al. influence-function-based CV inference, Benkeser et al. asymptotic equivalence, and van der Laan/Luedtke treatment-rule estimation literature; added summary text justifying CV-based inference.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Generalizability: The authors have not demonstrated that their results are generalizable. It remains unclear how the model would perform on data from countries not included in the training set, raising concerns about its broader applicability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors applied ABCD-learned rules to GEMS (different study, 6 years earlier, observational, including The Gambia and Mozambique sites not in ABCD); pattern preserved.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Inconsistencies in Reporting: In line 142, the percentage of children with recommendations (27.8%) differs from the value reported in Table 1. Similar discrepancies are noted for other outcomes and should be clarified.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that results text used average across seeds while Table 1 used median seed for descriptive analyses; added footnote and methods explanation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Explainability of the Rule: The proposed rule lacks explainability, which limits its interpretability and potential adoption in clinical settings.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised introduction to clarify the goal is to identify which data types determine treatment benefit, and added discussion that the rule could be adopted via mobile application without requiring full transparency.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Comparison with Existing Guidelines: In line 84, the authors mention that WHO recommends antibiotics for cases of bloody stool. It would be helpful to compare the performance of their comprehensive rule with the WHO guidelines to assess added value.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained ABCD trial excluded bloody-stool patients (lack of equipoise), making WHO comparison infeasible; noted as direction for future research.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The one thing I suggest the authors change is that I wonder if the n=6,692 is a bit misleading? in the main text it seems a much smaller number of children were included in the analysis for this paper.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that all 6,692 children were retained via nuisance regression handling missing outcomes; explained mechanism in revised main text.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please also present 'number needed to treat': to avoid diarrhoea on day 3, to avoid 1 hospitalisation or death.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added NNT (10 for day-3 diarrhea reduction; 42 for hospitalization/death reduction) in revised text.

reviewer_strengths.text: Relevant study. Important field. ABSTRACT reads well. Otherwise good abstract with absolute numbers, percentages, 95%CIs. Relevant outcomes, Authors present study limitations already in the abstract.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Two rounds, two main reviewers (Reviewer #1 fully accepted in Round 2 with 'no further comments'). The cross-validation-based-inference concern is a sophisticated methodological discussion that the authors handled by citing the influence-function CV literature; this is worth preserving as a pattern. External-dataset application to GEMS is a textbook example of substantive external validation added in response to peer review.

proposed_updates.paper_title: The Helicobacter pylori AI-clinician harnesses artificial intelligence to personalise H. pylori treatment recommendations

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The current study attempted to develop a H. pylori-AI clinician recommendation model for personalized treatment of H. pylori. However, this paper appears very immature without detailed information about the clinical features, lack of a comparison group (clinical decision or prior antibiotics exposure) as well as an external validation. What the investigators could demonstrate is the feasibility of building a model with dubious clinical value.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added external validation cohort of 7,186 patients from multiple European centers (Nov 2024-Mar 2025), demonstrated AI-recommended therapies outperformed clinician-prescribed (94.1% vs 88.1% internal; 92.8% vs 87.4% external), added LR baseline using resistance features (89.1%) for comparison.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The aim of the study was not properly defined and there was no pre-defined outcome. The so-called 100 binary variable features involved in building the model were not provided for evaluation. Methods for handling missing data should be outlined.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised abstract and introduction to define pre-defined objective (improving eradication rates vs clinician-prescribed), added full feature list to Supplementary Materials, outlined missing-data methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To enhance the credibility of the results, it is recommended to validate the model on external independent datasets from other centers.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors conducted external validation on 7,186 patients from multiple European centers (Nov 2024-Mar 2025); AI again outperformed (92.8% vs 87.4%).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To ensure compliance with reporting guidelines such as the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) statement and MI-CLAIM criteria.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors fully aligned reporting with MI-CLAIM (checklist in Supplement).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The main issue pertains to the accuracy of the ground truth data, specifically in determining the success of eradication therapy. As many subjects only received one type of treatment, it becomes challenging to assess if the patient would have been successful with other treatments based on predicted results from the algorithm. To address this issue, it is suggested to have prospective patient validation and see how accurate the prediction is rather than again based on retrospective analysis of another cohort of patients.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: When reporting model performance, it is essential to include sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (PLR), negative likelihood ratio (NLR), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The link to the Bitbucket repository isn't working. Without access to the repo, verifying any of the author's claims is impossible. Therefore, assessing the usability of your software is also impossible. The repo they list is an 'Error 404—page not found'. They probably didn't make it public.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors made Bitbucket repository public.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of real-world data seems to be incorrect and misleading as only simulated data has been used. They only seem to have used the simulated data. What is the Hp-EuReg dataset? If they had the clinical dataset, they should have tested it on it as well as the simulated dataset. This is research work and not a tool for clinical routine use, and testing a system on the clinical dataset is critical to gauge the future potential clinical effectiveness.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that primary analyses are on real-world Hp-EuReg data (n=38,049) plus external validation (n=7,186); simulated data was used only for benchmarking/calibration. Authors moved former Figure 3 (synthetic-data validation) to Supplementary to avoid confusion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why did you choose DQN, and why did you modify it to ignore states? Please discuss this on a more mathematical level, because no justification is given in the text. Have you compared this to other methods? Random forests? Support vector machines? What makes isDQN superior, and can you quantify that? What is the motivation for ignoring subsequent states?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors provided mathematical rationale (outcomes observed once per patient, no evolving state, so standard Q-learning with next-state transitions does not apply; future-state term removed from Bellman equation). Compared isDQN to LR (88.3%), RF (88.3%), SVM (88.3%) — isDQN achieved 94.1%.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Explain how you added the noise. Since the inputs are binary, is it done by flipping bits? Most confusing is that you say that you achieve an accuracy of 72% at a noise level of 99% - how so? Moreover, how does that reflect a 'real-world' scenario?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors confirmed noise was added by random bit-flipping; framed 99%/72% as stress-test illustrating residual structure rather than realistic noise level.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The goal of this study isn't obvious; what problem are you aiming to solve? The manuscript would highly benefit from clearly defined metrics. For example, when you say that '65.5% of patients were consistently recommended a bismuth therapy...by more than half of the models, which we treat as a frequency threshold'... What does that mean? Where does that leave the reader? You need to spell out all accuracy metrics for these numbers to make any sense.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised abstract/methods to state central research question (whether AI improves eradication rates), clarified that percentages reflect consistency of AI recommendations across 50 model runs.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: With a slightly higher 5.4% (92.8% vs. 87.4% eradication success), it is incorrect to say that the AI-clinician outperformed the standard clinician's decisions. The language could be revised.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Related to the splitting ratio for the training/testing sets, it would be great if the paper considered other scenarios. What happens if the splitting ratio is 70%/30% and 80%/20%?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not extracted in available pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Constructing an AI-clinician method for H. Pylori infection can be considered a new contribution to the research community. However, the method development in this manuscript only uses a Deep Q-Network Learning method for experiments. It would be great if the paper could compare other techniques to make the results more convincing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added LR, RF, SVM comparisons (88.3% each) vs isDQN (94.1%).

reviewer_strengths.text: This paper presented a new approach to constructing an AI-based platform that supports clinicians by recommending relevant treatments for patients with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection. Reinforcement learning method based on Deep Q-network learning is a novel application.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Two rounds. Reviewer #2 caught a critical reporting issue (paper read as if only simulated data were used; real-world Hp-EuReg use was unclear) — authors moved the synthetic-validation figure to supplement. Reviewer #1's Round-2 counterfactual concern (only one treatment per patient, can't observationally verify what other treatments would have done) is a deep RL-for-treatment-selection issue that doesn't have a clear resolution. Eradication-rate improvement is modest (5.4% absolute) — reviewer flagged language overclaim in Round 2.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Developing serum proteomics based prediction models of disease progression in ADPKD

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Authors aimed to examine the potential of serum proteomics for improved risk stratification in ADPKD, as indicated in the abstract. However, data interpretation, as stated in the abstract, is not supported by results: authors cannot exclude that changes in serum proteome of ADPKD patients are the effect of eGFR decline per sé, in fact the study does not include a control group of patients with variable eGFR due to other causes.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added separate IgA nephropathy CKD control cohort (Figure S4, Table S10), included eGFR in multivariate models to control for collinearity, showed proteome markers retain independent predictive capacity, and added eGFR-dependency analyses within the ADPKD cohort (Table S9).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: eGFR slope calculation: Authors estimated annual eGFR slope. Please define the mean/median period of observation for the definition of mean annual eGFR decline.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Table S1 detailing eGFR availability and timeframe (median follow-up 6.8/6.4/6.0 years; median 10/9/7 measurements; median intervals).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Identification of proteins associated with annual GFR slope: the authors indicate 4 serum proteins related to eGFR decline. In lines 187-88, authors comment 'highlighting their potential significance in the pathophysiology of renal function deterioration'. The study is not designed to show the causal relationship between serum changes and eGFR decline: the changes may represent the effect of eGFR decline.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors deleted pathophysiology wording and added limitations stating causality cannot be inferred; correlation analyses added.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Moreover, did the author correlate serum proteome to changes of renal volume? Besides eGFR decline, the increase in kidney volume is another parameter used in ADPKD clinical studies to address disease progression.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained serial TKV is not standard care per ERA Statement; longitudinal TKV unavailable in cohort. Cross-sectional TKV deemed limited added value.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Model Validation: The adjusted R² is reported at 0.31. It would be beneficial for the authors to compare this with other models beyond the Mayo Imaging Classification to contextualize whether an R² of 0.31 is considered robust.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors contextualized adjusted R² of 0.31 against literature, noted that TKV-based gold-standard models also show similar or lower R² values, and that adding genotype data improved performance further.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Patient Stratification: Considering that younger patients may not exhibit an eGFR slope >3 despite being at risk of rapid progression, it is advisable to stratify patients based on observed GFR rates (fast vs. slow) and predicted risks using both the Mayo Imaging Classification and PROPKD scores. It would be insightful to align proteomics biomarkers thresholds with these known progression rates.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added comparison using >3 ml/min/1.73m² cutoff (Figure S9: AUC 0.82 Combined Model, 0.69 MIC); explained thresholds for untargeted proteomics are not feasible due to relative quantification.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clinical Application: A critical clinical question is the prediction of ESRD onset. The authors have predicted future eGFR but this information is relegated to a supplemental figure. Clarity on the accuracy and error of this prediction is needed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added RMSE accuracy metric, expanded figure 2D explanation, clarified ΔeGFR interpretation and provided detailed legend revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Proteomic Indicators: Is the mere presence of specific proteins indicative of a worse outcome? Establishing thresholds for these proteins, and correlating them with known biological activities in ADPKD, would enhance the utility of the findings. Furthermore, is it possible for each proteome to be predictive on its own?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained MS-based proteomics is relative quantification, not absolute; presented missingness analysis (FERMT3 19.4% missing; RARRES2 22.2% missing with negative eGFR-slope correlation); argued single proteins insufficient — multi-biomarker model required.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Impact of Therapy: In patients who received disease-modifying therapy, such as tolvaptan, were there any changes in the proteomics profile? This would be crucial for understanding the impact of such treatments on disease progression.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors checked subcohort of 20 patients on tolvaptan — no differentially regulated proteins detected (likely sample-size limited); flagged as future direction.

reviewer_strengths.text: The need of prediction models for CKD progression in ADPKD is with no doubts of high clinic relevance. The variability of kidney outcome among ADPKD individuals from the same family and the poor reliability of current prediction models made this study of high interest.

The proteomic model was compared to observed eGFR slopes and the Mayo Imaging Classification, a commonly used imaging-based stratification model. The cohorts appear representative of the ADPKD population.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Proteomics study — borderline MLGG scope per project memo (omics-adjacent), but the prediction-modeling concerns are directly mappable. The headline methodological concern is the definition-variable-style collinearity (eGFR is both the target slope and a correlate of the candidate features — MLGG-F04 / definition_variable_guard); reviewer #1 raised this as the first concern and authors addressed via separate CKD control cohort plus eGFR adjustment in multivariate models. Two rounds; both reviewers accepted in Round 2.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Comprehensive interaction modeling with machine learning improves prediction of disease risk in the UK Biobank

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: UK Biobank has individuals who have kinship that is known to cause inflation for prediction models (Ellis 2024 AJHG). Since the model is fitting many predictors, there is a chance that the model is capturing subtle population structures that cross-validation could not remove. One solution is finding an external validation cohort; the other solution is making sure individuals in the training and testing don't have kinship (i.e. the same family are always in the training OR testing).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors restructured training/testing to use England+Wales for training and Scotland for testing as a proxy for external validation, and additionally excluded from the test set individuals sharing kinship (≥0.0442 coefficient, third-degree or closer) with any training-set member. Predictive performance remained stable under both stricter setups.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The c-index improvement is small and not easily interpretable (i.e. improvement from 0.6 to 0.7 has a very different interpretation than 0.7 to 0.8; even the same C-index with different incidence rate is not comparable). Is it possible to quantify the contribution of prediction power by the interaction terms (analogous to R2)? Previous study has shown that for traits with many small effects, non-additive variance is small.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added an incremental R² measure (ΔR²) based on Royston's R² for survival models and reported both incremental C-index and incremental R² in revised Figure 1, Table 1, and Supplementary Table 4.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Line 363 / Line 488 — what are the procedures for selecting hyperparameters? Line 494 mentioned grid search but did not specify what are the criteria used (is it based on cross validation of likelihood? Prediction C-index?).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Clarified that regularization parameters are selected based on the maximum C-index across the validation folds; updated both Methods (lines 607-617) and main text (lines 140-142).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please provide more details on how prevalent cases were excluded. How did you exclude the prevalent diseases listed in ST2? Some of the diseases don't have primary care data available.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added details on endpoint construction and prevalent-case exclusion (lines 117-121, 575-584): endpoints built from primary care, hospital episode statistics, death registries, self-reported diseases (first occurrences field 1712), plus cancer registry for lung cancer. Prevalent cases excluded based on first recorded occurrence before baseline assessment.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Line 495: How is the number of latent factors chosen, and how does the number of latent factors affect the predictive performance?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Adopted k=10 with L2 regularization; added Supplementary Figures 20-23 sweeping k showing performance plateaus at k=5-10. Discussion added at lines 457-470.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Line 160 and Table S4: absolute R2 values range from 24.9% to 95.0%, which seems very high. Is this due to the specific properties of Royston's R2?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified properties of Royston's R² (response captured in round-2 reply).

new_fields._extraction_notes: Survival/Cox extension with factorization-machine interactions. Borderline MLGG scope (survival outcomes vs binary), but reviewer concerns map cleanly to MLGG dimensions: kinship-induced leakage (S01-adjacent), hyperparameter selection (M03), endpoint construction (cohort definition). Reviewer #2 only co-reviewed; Reviewer #4 round-1 raised mostly framing/style critiques (no substantive MLGG items extracted). Reviewer #3 round-2 reported satisfaction.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Large language model powered knowledge graph construction for mental health exploration

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How do the authors plan to visualize the KG and deliver to the users? Currently, the github is not available. The code is not available at the github site.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors made the GitHub repository public (https://github.com/MonsterTea/MDKG) with README and Python code execution instructions; Reviewer #3 confirmed availability in round 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the MDD study, how is the 2000 individual control chosen? Also, why choose MDD? This procedure seems to be standardized across other mental health disorders as well — to show robustness, maybe the authors could experiment on other diseases as well.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors addressed control selection and discussed generalizability of pipeline to other diseases.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why is air pollution an important factor for MDD? Why do non-medical EHR embedding have such a good performance? Is there potential confounders? How do you select these variables to avoid confounders?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors addressed confounder selection rationale and feature provenance in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Use of ChatGPT: While ChatGPT demonstrates impressive performance across many benchmarks, the choice of a closed, proprietary platform for constructing a shared knowledge graph is problematic. A key expectation for a knowledge graph project is that it should be built on an openly available large language model (LLM), rather than a closed system like OpenAI's platform. The use of closed systems hinders transparency in understanding the deeper structures of the knowledge graph, raising concerns about the potential for data misuse by third-party providers.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors retained ChatGPT/GPT-4o but added confidence scoring, contradiction handling, and human evaluation correlation (mean r=0.78). Reviewer #2 still found justification insufficient in round 2 but accepted the revision overall.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Reliability of Insights: There is a lack of clarity regarding how users can verify the reliability of insights derived from the knowledge graph, particularly those not covered by established medical databases. It is crucial when employing LLMs that users are encouraged to critically assess machine-generated content rather than blindly trust it. Hallucinations — a known issue in many domains involving LLMs — pose a specific risk. How has this been addressed or mitigated in the current implementation?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added a Confidence Score (combining prediction score, impact factor, frequency, distinct years, recency, contradiction penalty) detailed in Appendix C; manual evaluation showed mean correlation 0.78 with human-assigned scores.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why have the authors focused on the use of PheCode over ICD-10? The authors include a line in the manuscript, however it needs more explanation. For an application of this research, would not prediction on ICD-10 codes be more meaningful?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors argued PheCodes avoid billing-practice confusion. Reviewer #2 in round 2 remained unconvinced and suggested simpler alternative (first two digits of ICD-10).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clarification of 'Disease Prediction': The use of the term 'disease prediction' remains ambiguous. It is unclear if the authors are predicting future diagnoses or simply identifying patients already labeled with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) in their dataset. The authors must explicitly clarify if their approach involves genuine predictive modeling — predicting future onset of disease — or merely labeling existing diagnoses accurately.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Response not captured in available PDF pages; flagged for human follow-up.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clarification Regarding AUC Values: The authors mention an improvement in AUC values (abstract) 'from 0.02 to 0.21.' This statement remains unclear and potentially misleading. Typically, an AUC value below 0.5 indicates a model performing worse than random chance, with meaningful AUC values typically ranging from 0.5 (random chance) to 1.0 (perfect classification). Thus, an AUC improvement to 0.21 is confusing and suggests either a typographical error or a conceptual misunderstanding.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Response not captured in available PDF pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I am confused on the claim around interpretability — primarily around the response for model selection and the SHAP analysis. The following statement in the rebuttal: 'We selected SVM and LR models as our primary approaches due to their interpretability and simplicity' is contradictory to another statement: 'Given the inherent instability of embeddings — meaning that feature correspondence across different training runs is not fixed — interpreting individual dimensions remains a challenge.'
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Response not captured in available PDF pages.

new_fields._extraction_notes: LLM-powered knowledge graph for mental health, with downstream UKB MDD prediction using SVM/LR/XGBoost/RF. Mixed scope — KG construction is out-of-scope but the UKB prediction task is in MLGG scope. Extracted concerns focus on prediction-relevant items (cohort, outcome coding, AUC reporting, interpretability, reproducibility). Some Reviewer #2 round-2 author responses were beyond the 10 pages I read; marked resolved=null.

proposed_updates.paper_title: A large-scale human toxicogenomics resource for drug-induced liver injury prediction

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The model was trained by RNA-seq data of sandwich-cultured primary human hepatocytes with a short-term exposure (24 hours). The severe distortions of two-dimensionally cultured hepatocyte gene expression due to de-differentiation has been clearly reported. Moreover, a short time exposure might not be sufficient to mimic many idiosyncratic toxicities that typically occur only after multiple weeks to months. Will such a selection bias of training data cause biased mechanistic prediction of the DILI candidates? This should at least be discussed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Acknowledged 2D-culture limitations; added Suppl. Fig. S2 showing hepatocyte marker expression confirming identity at 24h; added discussion section noting that 'the exposure timepoint of 24 hours limit the detection of delayed or immune-mediated toxicities.'

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why did the authors set the safety margin at 80? Is it an empirical value? Please specify the rationale of setting this value as cut-off since SMs of 30 are chosen in many other studies.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: MOS threshold of 80 selected by empirical optimization on held-out training data balancing sensitivity and specificity; clarified rationale in Results and Methods; threshold within literature range 10-100. Added Suppl. Fig. S5 panel B.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The numbers of drugs are not consistent and confusing across the manuscript and supplementary data files. While DILImap was claimed to include 300 drugs, the Results section mentions 177 DILI+ and 93 DILI- in the training set and 32 DILI+ and 14 DILI- in the validation data, which are 316 drugs. Supplementary Table shows a total of 299 drugs 'DILIMAP_RESULTS'.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified dataset counts and reconciled supplementary tables in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the modeling process, it is unclear whether the cross-validation mode was done for using all drugs in DILImap or only the training data. No details on how the training and validation datasets were constructed/split were given. What approach was taken to minimize potential biases in the validation set? This information would be particularly important with the claimed 100% specificity.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Clarified that 5-fold stratified compound-level cross-validation was used (described as 'all samples from a single compound were held out together'). Reviewer #3 in round 2 acknowledged this as 'clear and appropriate for preventing data leakage' but asked for further wording polish.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Despite extensive comparisons with various assays, the study does not benchmark ToxPredictor against other computational models, such as DILIPredictor, DILIGeNN, etc., for the same drugs. No rationale or supporting data were presented when choosing random forest as the algorithm.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added benchmarking against state-of-the-art in silico models per response letter; clarified RF rationale in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why 30-fold cross-validation was chosen? This fold seems very high considering the small dataset of 300 drugs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that 30-fold refers to ensembling (30 trained RF models), not stratified k-fold; subsequently revised wording to '30 models' / '30 ensemble members'.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Codes and data files were available through figshare and code ocean but not completely with many missing data files (e.g. DILImap_deseq2.h5ad). Please ensure all data files are provided.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Released full codebase via GitHub and PyPI, complete validation and processed training data, S3 bucket for reviewer access during peer review (with credentials provided in rebuttal).

new_fields._extraction_notes: DILImap toxicogenomics RNA-seq + Random Forest DILI prediction. Borderline omics scope, but extracted concerns focus on ML governance items applicable to MLGG (split protocol, threshold choice, sample-size, reproducibility, baseline comparison). Notable: rebuttal accidentally exposed AWS access keys in plaintext on the response page; not part of extraction but documented here for awareness. Reviewer #2 raised mostly biological-novelty critiques (not extracted as MLGG-substantive).

proposed_updates.paper_title: Artificial intelligence-driven metabolomics of retinal nerve fibre layer to profile risks of mortality and cardiometabolic diseases

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: RNFLT metabolic states are based on associations with RNFLT. However numerous eye diseases can also affect RNFLT. Were these eye diseases considered in the models? One concern is that the metabolic fingerprints were identified based on their association with RNFLT — which is affected by many ocular diseases; adjustment for these ocular conditions (glaucoma for example) is encouraged.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Implemented predefined exclusions of glaucoma, retinal disease, neurodegenerative disease, low signal-strength scans, high refractive error, etc., from the RNFLT-biomarker identification cohort. Updated Methods page 16 line 459.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The study's biggest limitation is lack of reproducibility. Without data and source code, the value of this study is significantly diminished and evaluation of the methodology is impossible. It's understandable that UKBB data can only be accessed through the established protocols. The validation data appears to be not accessible at all. At the very least, a working source code and simulated data should be made available.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors addressed code availability in revision; Reviewer #2 in round 2 acknowledged reasonable response.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Given the class imbalance in CMD outcomes, including Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) as a complementary metric (and associated baselines including a completely random/no-skill predictor) is critical.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added AUPRC as a complementary metric. Reviewer #2 in version 2 acknowledged 'refocusing the manuscript on AUPRC as the primary metric has made this a stronger article.'

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How should the magnitude of the improvement in predictive power (compared to baseline) be interpreted from an application/clinical standpoint? Are these improvements clinically relevant? A simulation study of benefits from such an improvement would be very valuable.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added clinical-impact discussion and reframed interpretation; Reviewer #2 round 2 noted 'concerned that the new Supplementary Table S13 demonstrates very limited improvements compared to baseline.'

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Link between RNFLT is tenuous since all metabolites are associated with CMD (and they don't show that RNFLT is associated with incident CMD); this likely reflects confounders that are not accounted for in the models (HTN, BP, individual prevalent CMD, HgA1C, HDL).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added confounder adjustment in fully-adjusted primary models; Reviewer #3 in round 2 still asked for these to be primary (not supplemental) and noted the result robustness primarily holds for DM, not hard incident CVD.
