reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The majority of the increase in c-statistics is minimal (0.02) except for DM when compared to more robust models like FHS, so not clinically meaningful, but it's not even clear from Fig 2 if they are statistically significant changes?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added significance testing and re-presented Figure 2; round-2 reviewers still flagged that 5/6 baselines remained within CI of proposed models.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How was prevalent CVD/DM addressed? Need to use 'European ancestry' instead of 'Caucasian ethnicity' (as the latter was not specifically addressed in UKB); shouldn't use 'diabetic patients' (instead should use 'patients with diabetes'). Need to adjust for multiple testing for incident CMD including the number of tests at the level of number of CMD tested.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised terminology, added multiple-testing adjustment, and clarified prevalent-case exclusion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors are commended for using several population groups in their analysis. The datasets include mainly Chinese and White individuals. The lack of representation of Black individuals should be mentioned in the discussion as a limitation to this study.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Added explicit limitation in Discussion and Abstract conclusion on under-representation of Black individuals.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Metabolomics + RNFL OCT → CMD risk prediction (Cox models). Borderline omics+imaging scope, but the predictive-modeling concerns (AUPRC, calibration, confounding, definition-variable risk where RNFLT defines both feature and outcome pathway) are squarely MLGG-relevant. Multiple unresolved concerns where round-2 reviewers remained skeptical of clinical relevance.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Genetic profiling of the circulating proteome in common diseases suggests causal proteins and improves risk prediction

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clinically, the usefulness of risk models is to identify those at high risk of disease in the future, or in some clinical contexts for the diagnosis of disease that is not yet clinically manifest. Since genotype is static, it can make sense to do risk modeling using genotype data on those who already have disease compared to healthy controls. However, protein levels are not static. Did the risk modeling only include those who were disease-free at baseline?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Confirmed that risk modeling was conducted specifically among disease-free individuals at baseline; prevalent cases excluded for incident-disease evaluation. Documented in Methods 'Disease-risk prediction with different risk scores' section, page 27.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors chose to focus on incident diseases only, omitting prevalent diseases. What is the rationale for omitting proteomic associations with prevalent diseases (i.e., diseases diagnosed at the time of blood draw)?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Focusing on incident cases ensures proteomic measurements precede disease onset, avoiding reverse causation. This follows fundamental temporal sequence of cause-preceding-effect, reducing bias and enabling direct estimation of disease risk.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: While proteomic risk scores may have significant clinical potential, their practical adoption faces challenges similar to the 'black box' nature of genomic data. The study does not address this aspect of clinical translation. We suggest acknowledging this limitation and proposing future strategies for feature reduction, possibly focusing on a smaller set of proteins, such as 20 or 30.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: In revision, number of high-confidence proteins used for disease risk prediction was reduced to less than 30 per disease, providing a foundation for clinically feasible implementation (Fig. 5D, Table S21).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I'm unclear on how the sample sizes for each disease were derived. While I see the ICD-10 codes listed in ST1, the sample sizes as detailed in ST4 are smaller than I would expect. For example, 132 Parkinson's cases are listed, but when I check the values listed by Sun et al.1, for just one of the Parkinson's related ICD-10 codes (G20, see ST2 in that manuscript), they list 342 cases in just the randomized baseline portion of the samples. Given both manuscripts utilize the UKB-PPP, why does this discrepancy exist between the studies?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified case derivation and discrepancy with Sun et al. in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Throughout the manuscript, the authors focus on the raw number of significant variants instead of on the number of unique associations. While describing the total number of variants associated with protein levels initially is fine, the numbers generally become meaningless. For example, the authors say that 30 associations were identified in lung cancer. Does this represent 30 independent pQTLs, or is this 30 variants, all of which are in the same LD block associated with one protein? I would suggest that instead of focusing on the total number of variants, the authors instead focus on the number of independent associations in all analyses beyond the initial paragraph.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified independent vs total association counts and revised presentation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Figure 4A: How can 89.74% of breast cancer pQTLs be disease-specific and 89.21% be health-specific at the same time? Line 287/Figure 4E/F: How was pathway analysis performed? Again, if the background gene set was not set properly, these results may be invalid.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified percentage calculation and pathway-analysis background gene set.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The main hypothesis of the study is that disease-related pQTLs are present only under certain disease conditions, and thus the pQTL analysis is performed in case-only cohorts for several diseases using the prevalent cases for each disease. Based on the hypothesis, the changes in the protein levels would be the effect or consequences of the disease pathophysiology. However, the authors have further assessed the causality of the proteins using the incident cases and MR analysis. Authors also used the identified pQTLs to predict the diseases. These downstream analyses do not align with the primary hypothesis of the study.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified the conceptual flow between case-only pQTL discovery and downstream causality/prediction analyses.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How did the authors account for the co-morbidity of the included diseases. What was the proportion of co-occurrence of the diseases in the cohort?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors addressed comorbidity handling in revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There are huge differences in the sample sizes across the diseases (varying from 55 to 12,000 individuals), and hence statistical power for the discovery of pQTLs, which could be one of the potential reasons for differences in the number of identified pQTLs across the diseases. Many of the pQTLs for diseases with large cohort may have not been identified in other diseases due to the smaller sample size (false negative). Could the authors check the significance level of the pQTLs identified in diseases with larger cohort such as hypertension and/or in healthy cohort in the diseases with smaller cohorts. I would suggest having a threshold of minimum number of cases for a disease to be included in the study and restrict the analysis to such diseases.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors addressed power differences across diseases and clarified minimum case threshold.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Line 392: The C-indices for models with PRS and without PRS are very similar for most of the diseases (Fig 6B), indicating that addition of PRS to the ProRS doesn't add to the prediction. Thus the conclusion that integrating genetic and proteomic data refines predictive accuracy is not correct.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised conclusion language; round 2 reviewers accepted overall.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Proteomics (pQTL + PRS + ProRS) with Cox-based risk prediction across 42 diseases in UKB. Borderline omics scope but the prediction-task concerns (incident vs prevalent, cohort definition, C-index added value, sample-size variation) map cleanly to MLGG dimensions. Reviewer #2 round 2 raised additional region-definition/pathway issues; Reviewer #3 round 2 satisfied.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Congenital heart disease detection by pediatric electrocardiogram based deep learning integrated with human concepts

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: All children in the study underwent ECG. The authors should provide further comment on the indications for this ECG – I assume that an ECG is not performed routinely (i.e., among patients in whom CHD is not suspected), and therefore the presence of an ECG for clinical purposes is subject to indication bias. This is a substantial limitation since it becomes unclear how the model would perform when applied prospectively among individuals who would not necessarily otherwise get an ECG (such as those who could be 'screened' for CHD as the authors suggest as a primary use case).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the indication bias, removed 'CHD screening' claims, and added a limitation noting the cohort came from a real-world referral context, not from screening of general pediatric population.
reviewer_concerns._qc_flag: QC flag: author_response overstates concession; reviewer C01 actually defended framing

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clarification of phenotyping is needed. Specifically, reference is made to CHD detection 'following the standard guideline with various tools', but no reference or guidelines are provided, and the description is vague. A clearer definition of how each CHD was defined would be useful.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that diagnostic workup followed the ESC Guidelines for CHD (primarily transthoracic echocardiography + ECG), cited the 2020 ESC guideline reference, and clarified attending-physician final adjudication.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Is there any assessment of model calibration? How accurate are the predicted probabilities on an absolute basis? This is a fundamental component of model evaluation that appears lacking.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Brier score as a calibration measure to Table 1; reported values close to 0 indicating good calibration. They added explanation in Results.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors argue that the deep learning model is more sensitive to CHD diagnosis than the cardiologists. This is only showing one side of the story (i.e., does the increase in sensitivity come at a cost of lower specificity), and is therefore incomplete. A standard NRI analysis would be more customary and balanced.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors reorganized cardiologist comparison using NRI metric across 10 randomly sampled test groups; in round 2 added NRI(+) and NRI(-) components as suggested.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors should consider displaying precision-recall curves in addition to ROC.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added precision-recall curves to Fig.1 and PR-AUC values to supplementary tables, noting label imbalance considerations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The proportion of tracings excluded for 'corruption' is very high (40% in Ref A and 50% in Ref B). This is concerning, and may be a source of bias. More detail is needed regarding assessment of tracing quality and criteria for excluding tracings based on noise. Ideally an objective definition would be applied.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified definition: ECG data with >20% signal amplitudes exceeding 5 mV or >20% recorded values of 0; clarified that signal corruption is common in pediatric ECG; revised Methods to make exclusion criteria explicit and unrelated to CHD status.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors argue that a potential value of the CHDdECG model is better detection of CHD in resource-poor settings, but the model was not evaluated in such settings (i.e., it was evaluated in two large tertiary care centers). I would also acknowledge geographic specificity of train/test as a potential limitation to generalizability.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added a sentence about geographic and temporal specificity as a limitation; in round 2 added a third external validation cohort from Northeast China (Center-C, ~2300 km away, different ECG device brand).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For data pre-processing, the authors normalized the three types of features using z-score. However, this approach will eliminate true amplitude for QRS-complex, which is the supportive evidence for some morphology anomaly. The authors should provide the reason for ignoring the amplitude information.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors justified z-score normalization for stable DL training, argued absolute amplitudes were linearly scaled and that DL models extract patterns rather than rely on raw amplitude; expert reviewers noted preferred handling.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Please add ablation study for utilizing Xe, Xw and Xc as feature input separately. And the authors should discuss the effectiveness and rationality of using the three feature extraction methods according to the ablation results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added an ablation study (Fig. S1) comparing single and combined feature modalities (ECG signal, clinical, wavelet); showed all-three combination outperforms individual modalities, particularly on recall.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although I agree the disease labels used in this study are likely of good quality, I would nevertheless acknowledge the possibility of label misclassification as a limitation. As the authors argue, CHD can be present with ECG abnormalities below the level of human detection, and since many patients were included after having ECGs performed for non-cardiac indications, it is possible that some of these patients labeled as non-CHD actually had CHD that was never diagnosed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added label misclassification as a stated limitation in the Discussion section, noting the need for a prospective protocol with standardized diagnostic workup for all individuals.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A more precise external validation is necessary. I suggest obtaining and using external validation data from another country or a different device company. Alongside AUROC, the authors should also describe the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acquired an additional external test set from Northeast China (Center-C, 2300 km from Guangzhou) with a different ECG device brand (NIHON KOHDEN ECG-2550 vs GE MAC800); added AUROC and PR-AUC across all three test sets.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I would like the authors to verify whether any patients from the external validation data set were included in the training data set. If so, how can this be ensured?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors excluded Center-B patients already present in Center-A using the enterprise master patient index (EMPI) with age, date of birth, sex, and name; for Center-C, used spatial distance and patient-info comparison to ensure non-overlap. Clarification added to Methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors are requested to elucidate the process of model structure selection and the training process for the final model. Can the authors affirm with certainty that, among various models or structures considered, the final model selected is indeed the most accurate? Furthermore, should the deep learning model using waves prove to be more advanced, the necessity of employing wavelets of clinical features may be eliminated. In this context, the authors need to ponder whether such a process could lead to overfitting accuracy.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors detailed model structure selection process: ablation study (Fig S1), comparison with classical models (CNN, LSTM, kNN, XGBoost, RF) in Tables S3-S4, and justified wavelet branch with information-preference references; argued strong external test performance suggests against overfitting.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The developed model's accuracy should be checked further in terms of stratification by patient age, sex, and heart rate. Additionally, the authors should provide a baseline characteristics table for the patient cohort.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added stratified performance analysis (Table S5) by sex, age, and heart rate across all three cohorts, with ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Spec, Sens, Brier; added baseline characteristics in Table S2.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Three reviewers across 2 review rounds (Rev #1 + #2 in R1, Rev #1 + #3 in R2; Rev #2 not in R2). Round 3 R1 and R3 both confirmed acceptance. Strong methodological revision trajectory.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Artificial intelligence-enabled prediction of chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity from baseline electrocardiograms

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It appears the goal was to predict underlying left ventricular pathology (subclinical or concealed) prior to initiation or chemotherapy. Given CTRCD is believed to be caused by the chemotherapeutic regimen, it seems unlikely that we will be able to predict this future event before the inciting factor is actually introduced. It brings up the question of - what is the model actually predicting? I suspect the AI-EF model likely just predicts an overall poor LV substrate and susceptibility to any adverse exposures and as such is not necessarily specific for CTRCD.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified the model detects baseline cardiac abnormalities determining susceptibility to cardiotoxic agents (not CTRCD per se); revised abstract, discussion, and conclusions; built new AI-CTRCD model via transfer learning specifically trained on patients receiving anthracyclines.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Did the authors consider just using the model to detect the presence of CTRCD once it develops? ECGs taken after the initiation of chemotherapy could contain information about the damage caused specifically by the chemotherapy and thus could improve the prediction.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors evaluated post-chemotherapy ECGs in 787 patients and found AI-EF score still stratified CTRCD risk (HR 2.64); acknowledged selection bias in post-chemo ECGs (symptomatic patients) and added clarification in Discussion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the specific prediction of CTRCD, perhaps the authors might need to consider training and evaluating a new model among patients who have actually begun chemotherapy. I realize the authors have pointed out a limitation related to sample size with doing this, but perhaps their ability to successfully collaborate with multiple institutions based on their publication regarding the AI-EF model derivation (ref 26) and potential use of generative adversarial networks could help address the limited sample size.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors collaborated with Keio University Hospital (Japan) to add 190 chemotherapy patients; retrained the AI-EF model via transfer learning specifically for CTRCD prediction (AI-CTRCD model); revised tables and figures.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The AUC of 0.77 vs. 0.75 seems to be a marginal improvement in performance with addition of the AI-EF to model to known risk factors. Although this difference was shown to be statistically significant, one can argue that it might not necessarily be clinically important. The clinical risk factors model appears to do well on its own (AUV 0.75). Can the authors provide an AUC for the AI-EF model by itself to see if using the ECG alone would be sufficient for prediction if other clinical variables/risk factors are not readily available.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added AUROC for AI-CTRCD alone (0.672), a 4-variable model with AI (0.750), and deployment simulation showing detection of 32 additional CTRCD cases at fixed echo capacity; rephrased significance language throughout.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the results section, the authors mention that 1,138 individuals were enrolled. Were these patients prospectively enrolled or did the authors simply mean that data on these patients were extracted from electronic health records? If the latter, would suggest re-wording to avoid confusion.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that 1,138 individuals were retrospectively identified from MGB EDW, not prospectively enrolled; updated wording in Results and Methods.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors state that the 'AI-EF model demonstrated excellent stratification of the risk of CRTCD' and I was wondering how this was determined? Based on the hazard ratio? an AUC of 0.77, a positive predictive value of 16.9%? I would not consider any of these 'excellent stratification' and this sentence seems overstated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors rephrased 'excellent stratification' to 'The AI-CTRCD model stratified the baseline risk of CTRCD using ECG.'

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: When evaluating the performance of the AI-EF model, did the authors make sure that the patients included in the cohort presented in this manuscript were not included in the original training and validation cohorts given their prior paper (ref 26) discussing model derivation mentions that data was obtained from BWH, MGH, UCSF, and Keio.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors found a minor overlap; developed a new AI-EF model excluding the study population ECGs from training, demonstrated equivalent AUROC (0.91 BWH; 0.89 MGH; 0.91 UCSF; 0.92 Keio); used the new model for transfer learning.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Did the authors consider sex-based stratification when evaluating the performance of the 2 models described given, we know that there are sex-based differences in cardiovascular outcomes?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added sex-stratified subgroup analysis (Fig 3C, 3D): male HR 2.54 (95%CI 1.41-4.58), female HR 2.70 (95%CI 1.43-5.12); both significant.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: 7.1% in the low AI-EF score group developed anthracycline-related cardiomyopathy vs. 8.9% overall and 12.9% in the high AI-EF score group; alternatively expressed, 41 of the 99 patients who developed anthracycline-related cardiomyopathy had a low-risk score. While the hazard model appears promising, the prognostic performance, the differential ability to stratify into truly low risk and truly high risk by the AI-ECG algorithm for low EF does not seem to be as strong.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors re-calculated with new AI-CTRCD model: HR 2.66, incidence rate 8.94 vs 3.09 per 100 person-years; using full model with clinical variables, ~7-fold risk difference, and explained model is meant to be used with clinical variables in a combined prediction.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Retrospective datasets always pose a challenge; how many of the patients did have a pre- and post-therapy echocardiogram or EF assessment that would allow for robust adjudication of primary event rate?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors found 581 patients (57.5%) had both pre- and post-therapy LVEF assessment; HR 2.43 still observed; added analysis and limitations in Discussion noting potential bias from missing follow-up echos.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the reporting of the anthracycline dose, cumulative doxorubicin equivalents is the most commonly reported and might be worth changing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added cumulative doxorubicin equivalents reporting; ran additional Cox analysis using cumulative dose (HR 1.97 [1.24-3.12]); justified using initial dose for prediction (cumulative dose not available at chemo start); added stratified analysis by cumulative dose subgroups.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Round 2 added Reviewer #3 with only minor reference-update concerns. Major leakage/overlap concern (C07) from R1 was addressed with model rebuild. C04 deployment simulation is a notable strength.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Large language models streamline automated machine learning for clinical studies

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It was not entirely clear if the revision addressed the prior reviewer comments about whether multiple repeat prompts were attempted to asses for consistency in ChatGPT ADA's behavior and choices of analysis.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors confirmed multiple repeat prompts in different chat sessions consistently produced the same ML model and parameter selections, with one exception under compute constraints; revised Discussion to clarify consistency assessment and lack of hallucinations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The revision could benefit from a sharper description of the previous reviewer's comments between the well-curated (trial) datasets used for testing compared to the real-world clinical data sources that are likely to have much more missingness and irregularities. Half the battle in clinical machine learning projects is typically the data pre-processing to get heterogeneous clinical data in irregular data formats into a well-structured data frame to enable the AutoML process.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors revised Limitations section to explicitly acknowledge gap between well-curated trial datasets and real-world clinical data, noting more advanced preprocessing would be needed and ChatGPT ADA's effectiveness in that setting remains to be assessed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: As a more general presentation comment, many of the chat interaction screenshots (e.g. Figure 2) appear illegible at lower resolution when formatted into PDF. These need to be high resolution in publication, or better yet, consider simply including the text of the chat logs (as in the Supplementary material chat logs). These are essential to the value of this manuscript, as they provide the blueprint for readers to replicate the process in their own studies.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors converted all interactions to text format (Supplementary Notes 1-4), revised Fig.2 to include only key parts at higher resolution; removed redundant Supplementary Fig.1.

new_fields._extraction_notes: PDF includes editorial note that manuscript was previously reviewed at another journal; only revision-round comments included. Only 1 round of Nature Comm review. Rev #1 had a minor SHAP contextualization comment (resolved); Rev #3 had no remarks. The 3 substantive concerns are from Rev #2's second-pass evaluation.

proposed_updates.paper_title: A framework for evaluating clinical artificial intelligence systems without ground-truth annotations

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The experiments were conducted on two datasets, one of which (Multi-Domain Sentiment) is a general domain dataset that does not relate to clinical data. Further, the second dataset is constructed based on assumptions that do not guarantee the presence of 'in the wild' or 'distribution-shift' scenarios. The experimental evidence does not seem to be sufficient to make such claims. I would recommend using publicly available domain-shift datasets to validate the proposed solution, without being limited to NLP-only datasets.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added experiments on Stanford diverse dermatology images (DDI) dataset with documented distribution shift, and in round 2 added Camelyon17-WILDS histopathology benchmark. Showed SUDO correlates with model performance across modalities.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The proposed solution (SUDO) is explained in plain language as an algorithm; however, I find there is a lack of motivation and critical reasoning regarding potential corner cases where this algorithm could fail. For instance, the authors mention that deep neural nets can make class posterior predictions with very high confidence and still fail, which could render the inference probability estimates collected on 'in-the-wild' samples less meaningful. Therefore, the study requires more theoretical justification, along with additional experimental analysis, to support the claims made.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors conducted simulated-data stress tests varying distribution shift, class imbalance, third-class injection, and label noise. Showed SUDO continues to correlate with model performance in most scenarios but fails with drastic label noise or class-distribution flip; added 'Exploring the limits of SUDO with simulated data' section.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although the authors discuss related literature in identifying unreliable AI predictions in the introduction and reverse testing and validation in the conclusion, there are important gaps in the literature review with respect to evaluating model accuracy with scarce or no labeled data. It is necessary to draw connections with these works and characterize the contribution of this paper in light of these developments.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors incorporated suggested references (positive-unlabeled, semi-supervised, verification bias) into Introduction and Discussion; emphasized SUDO's data-centric (not model-centric) positioning and the gap in identifying unreliable predictions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Methods for statistical inference are neither provided nor discussed. For example, one would need procedures for statistical testing and interval estimation to evaluate algorithmic bias and to compare the area under the reliability completeness curve for two candidate models.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors positioned SUDO as upstream of statistical inference (providing ranking and bias flag); added Discussion paragraph that SUDO is one step in decision-making and subsequent statistical tests would be needed.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: SUDO relies on several hyperparameter and modeling choices, including the discretion into quantiles, the number of samples from each quantile, the choice of classifier, choice of discrepancy metric and threshold, etc. Can the authors provide more discussion and/or evaluation of the sensitivity of their method to these choices? What specific guidance can be provided to practitioners?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Fig.4) varying sample count (200 vs 50), classifier (logistic regression vs random forest), and label noise; SUDO correlation remained strong (|p|>0.94). Added Practical Guidelines for using SUDO (page 7).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The MultiSentiment dataset is used to illustrate the utility of SUDO. While I agree with the authors that this dataset is a good testing ground, the paper is motivated by the application of AI in medicine. It would be preferable for this analysis to be supplemental and for a publicly available medical dataset to be presented in the main text. For example, the MIMIC dataset (or potentially the MIMIC phenotype annotation dataset) is one option and well-known by the ML for health community.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors relegated MultiSentiment results to Supplementary and added Stanford DDI dataset to main text; pointed to response to Theme 1.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Will any code for SUDO be made publicly available?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Initially: 'Our code is currently undergoing a patent review and is thus not publicly available.' Round 2 response: Authors decided to open-source SUDO codebase at https://github.com/flatironhealth/SUDO. Code Availability statement updated.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The lack of statistical inference procedures is a major limitation and should at least be pointed out in the discussion section. Although the authors argue one can rank competing models with the reliability-completeness curve, without uncertainty estimates it is impossible to know if these rankings are trustworthy. The same issue arises when evaluating model fairness and in identifying unreliable predictions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors agreed and added to Discussion: SUDO is one of the first steps in decision-making; subsequent statistical significance tests would be needed for trustworthy conclusions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors partially addressed this concern by adding in the Stanford Dermatology dataset, as well as synthetic data, and thereby adding positive results on new datasets and outside the text domain. However, a significantly stronger case would have been made if the authors showed these results on in-the-wild suites/benchmarks (e.g. WILDS, a very popular 10-benchmark dataset including pathology + cell imaging), to take away any possibility of cherrypicking.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Camelyon17-WILDS histopathology benchmark experiment, showing SUDO correlation (p=-0.79) with model performance on hospital-shifted data.

For instance, in a scenario where the framework incorrectly diagnoses a skin condition, a patient might forego a doctor's visit. As time passes, the condition could deteriorate, leading to a delayed visit when treatment becomes more challenging. How does the framework intend to address such situations, ensuring the reliability of its diagnostic recommendations?

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: From Figure 4c, we can see reasonable consistency, but typically, in ML trained models, it is customary to provide other metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, accuracy, AUC and ROC curve etc. Can the authors comment on these metrics?

reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors discussed edge case handling and limitations of the validation set.

How was the process standardized, if at all, for the submission of such photos?

proposed_updates.paper_title: An explainable longitudinal multi-modal fusion model for predicting neoadjuvant therapy response in women with breast cancer

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The performance metrics within the genuinely independent dataset (i.e., the Duke cohort) leave much to be desired. Furthermore, the sample size of this independent dataset is notably small, particularly for certain subsets such as HER2+ or those receiving endocrine therapy, complicating the reliability of any derived conclusions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors' conclusion that the MRP could 'reduce unnecessary treatment toxicity in non-pCR cases by 35.8% without halting effective treatment in the Pre-NAT scenario, and potentially eliminate surgery for pCR cases by 16.7% without foregoing treatment opportunities in the Post-NAT scenario' is, in my view, flawed. This is because there is no established efficacy for altering therapy based on an anticipated lack of pCR. Moreover, forgoing surgery is not a current standard of care, and the necessity for prospective trials (some of which are currently underway) renders this conclusion somewhat misleading.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors moderated statements to acknowledge that hypothetical advantages require further testing/clinical trials; reframed as patient selection for enrollment in trials rather than direct treatment alteration.

reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added two additional external cohorts (Fujian Provincial Hospital cohort C and I-SPY2 cohort D) with longitudinal multi-modal data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The models used prior to neoadjuvant therapy (pre-NAT) appear to yield results comparable to those of other models that consider imaging during and after treatment. proposed_updates.paper_title: Multiplexed nanomaterial-assisted laser desorption/ionization for pan-cancer diagnosis and classification

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Looking at the age of the Healthy control group, it seems to be younger than other cancer groups, except PTC. As metabolome is highly influenced by many factors, including age, sex, and BMI, in a perfect situation, groups of patients being compared should be matched to these factors. No information about the participants' BMI is provided. Sex differences between HC and selected cancer groups are clearly observed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed subgroup analyses by age/sex/BMI within healthy controls showing no significant difference in the NALCI score, but did not match the actual case-control comparison.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: However, a detailed description of MS raw data treatment is missing, e.g., what was used to normalize the data? What was the reproducibility of the signals' measurement? The raw data preprocessing steps (code? algorithm?) are not provided for evaluation. What type of normalization process was applied?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors described the preprocessing pipeline (smoothing, baseline correction, alignment, TIC normalization) and added a flowchart figure.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Also the use of SVM, which generates an enormous number of higher order terms, none of which were specified in the analysis could cause problems. Given a mass spectrum containing hundreds of peaks, it's not hard to imagine that the classifier contains thousands of terms many of which are non-linear and which outnumber the number of samples. The problem is that when anything changes (and it will!) like the nano-material prep, the sample prep, the sample procurement protocol, the reaction products caused by laser irradiation of the sample, etc. it's easy for some of the non-linear terms to change dramatically, throwing off the algorithm.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors identified and validated 8 metabolite biomarkers with MS/MS to provide a chemical anchor, but did not retrain a classifier on the reduced feature set.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I don't think that the very high AUC values match with some of the sensitivity and specificity numbers provided. For example, it is not possible to generate an AUC of 0.99 using sensitivity=0.84 and specificity 0.84. The highest AUC could be in that situation is 1-(0.16)^2 = 0.97, but it could definitely be lower depending on the shape of the AUC curve. The authors need to double check their other AUC values as well.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained that their multi-class sensitivity definition differs from the binary one, showing how a multi-class confusion matrix produces lower per-class sensitivity than binary aggregation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors use the term 'metabolic fingerprints for pan-cancer diagnosis and classification', however no single metabolite is reported. This is in my opinion the weakest point of the manuscript. What is the identity of the top 30 or top 10 relevant m/z ions? MS/MS data is missing in that regard. In my opinion, the authors cannot sustain this method and a publication in Nature Communications on just mass spec features that could perfectly result from redundant signals from the same metabolite (isotopes, adducts, in-source fragments).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors identified 8 metabolite biomarkers with MS/MS confirmation, representing ~1/3 of the top signals.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Network-based machine learning approach to predict immunotherapy response in cancer patients

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Not all immune checkpoint inhibitors are the same, biomarkers likely different. This is reflected in analysis in the Liu et al paper (patients previously tx with aCTLA4 vs aPD1 naive patients) and different histologies. Overall, the authors bring together 700 quite heterogeneous datasets including different tumor types (unclear why these types chosen) with different immune checkpoint inhibitor treatments. reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Is (1) RECIST or not? For RECIST data, methods state aggregation: CR/PR and SD/PD - SD patients are often actually considered responders since they are non-progressing. Other datasets just used their R vs NR status (did that agree with CR/PR and SD/PD categories)? Should be the same across all data sets (and often these variables do differ across studies). Also OS is not a great marker for response to IO (patients will see many other lines of treatment), usually use PFS or even cancer-specific survival.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not explicitly addressed in the visible response text.

For how many patients was this 'method' used to determine the ground truth (response vs. non-response)?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not directly addressed in the visible response text.

reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not directly addressed in the visible response text.

reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not directly addressed in the visible response text.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Machine learning-based tissue of origin classification for cancer of unknown primary diagnostics using genome-wide mutation features

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A major technical limitation is that there is substantial imbalance in sample size in this dataset as reviewer 3 pointed out, and many cancer types and subtypes have insufficient sample sizes to conduct proper hold-out test and even cross-validation. The overall accuracy measure can be misleadingly high in cases with high imbalance of case and 'control'. The analysis should restrict to cancer types that have sufficient sample size. In addition, sensitivity and PPV should be reported as a more honest assessment of the classification performance. For rare cancer types a classifier should take into account of the prevalence of the disease.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified they calculated per-cancer-type accuracy (recall) rather than total accuracy, added sensitivity and PPV curves for each cancer type binary classifier (Supplementary figure 11), and showed sample-size table.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is some fundamental confusion on the definition of classification accuracy used in the study. The authors defined a per sample accuracy as (number of samples correctly predicted as breast) / (total number of breast samples). This is the definition of 'sensitivity' or 'recall', NOT 'overall accuracy'. The missing side of the equation is 'precision' or 'PPV' which is the fraction of actual breast cancer cases out of predicted breast cancer of origin. Both precisions and recalls should be reported in the main text and a direct comparison of these values to those reported in the published whole-genome TOO studies they cited in the paper (ref 6 and 7) would more convincingly show the added value of this study.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors replaced per-class 'accuracy' with 'recall', added precision/PPV numbers to Figure 2, included a comparison of CUPLR's precision to PCAWG-NN and Salvadores-SVM classifiers (Supplementary figure 10).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Despite the combined PCAWG and Hartwig cohort, the sample size is still far from sufficient to establish a classifier for all 30+ tumor types. The clinical utility is also unclear due to the limited availability of WGS in clinical setting.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the limitation, explained that CUPLR is intended to complement (not replace) other clinical evidence, and noted WGS is becoming a reimbursed diagnostic for CUP patients in the Netherlands since 2021.

new_fields._extraction_notes: WGS somatic mutations paper is OUT_OF_SCOPE per CLAUDE.md (omics modality); manuscript was previously reviewed at another journal so this PDF only contains the Nature Communications iteration (limited rounds visible). Reviewer #4 caught a fundamental metric-definition error (accuracy vs recall) — useful KB example. Resolution status confident based on visible author responses.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Unified classification and risk-stratification in Acute Myeloid Leukemia

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A concern bothers me that when talking about the mutations. The authors wrote that many of the patients were intensively treated. When were the biopsy were drawn? Would the molecular profiles of these patients be those before or after they were treated? There might be a lineage selection process during the patient journey. The authors confirm that molecular assessment of UK-NCRI is taken at diagnosis, but what about the validation AMLSG cohort?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors confirmed all samples were diagnostic and treatment-naive for both UK-NCRI and AMLSG cohorts; updated the manuscript to clarify the validation AMLSG cohort molecular assessment was also at diagnosis.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Editorial note states the manuscript was previously reviewed at another journal not operating a transparent peer-review scheme, so this PDF contains only the truncated Nature Communications iteration with very limited reviewer text. Reviewer #1 stated 'satisfactorily addressed the prior critiques'. Only one substantive concern about treatment-naive sampling visible. AML clinical+molecular data is borderline-scope (clinical with molecular features); kept in scope. Reviewer count of 2 reflects only those who left comments at this iteration.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Uncertainty-informed deep learning models enable high-confidence predictions for digital histopathology

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: On Page 3, lines 92 - 93, the authors stated 'we describe a clinically-oriented method for determining slide-level confidence using the Bayesian approach to estimating uncertainty, with uncertainty thresholds determined from training data'. I don't understand why the proposed method is a 'Bayesian approach'. The Section 'Estimation of Uncertainty' from lines 425 - 467 is quite confusing to me. A lot of notations are not well defined. For a Bayesian approach, what is the likelihood and what is the prior. How to compute the posterior? All those details are missing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors rewrote the 'Estimation of Uncertainty' section with improved notation clarity, referenced Gal et al. for the dropout-Bayesian equivalence, and added a new paragraph explaining BNN approach.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There are a lot of tuning parameters in the UQ-enable and non-UQ deep learning models, e.g., the dropout rate, the network architectures. It would be helpful if the authors provide some justifications on the choices of those parameters.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained hyperparameters were chosen from prior work (Dolezal, 2021) without further tuning to reduce overfitting risk, with the exception of added dropout layers and early stopping; added discussion of dropout rate choice rationale.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The imaging processing procedure may have large impact on the classification accuracy and uncertainty quantifications. In particular, the steps for removing background image tiles including grayspace fitering, Otsu's thresholding and gaussian blur detection. The authors should provide more details on those procedures and show the sensitivity of the UQ to the mild changes of tuning parameters in those procedures.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added detailed background-filtering procedure descriptions, ran an ablation across blur/Otsu/grayspace combinations (Supp Fig.6) and varied grayspace threshold (Supp Fig.7), showing UQ thresholding generalized across processing variants (P<0.001).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It would be helpful to include more discussion on low confidence predictions. For these predictions, one could not make any decision. Readers might be interested in learning how many are these low confidence cases. If there are too many, the proposed methods may not be that effect in practical applications.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion explaining ~1/4 of predictions are low-confidence, with a paragraph on application-specific tolerance trade-offs.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Histopathology WSI paper is OUT_OF_SCOPE per CLAUDE.md (imaging modality); however the reviewer concerns about Bayesian-method documentation, hyperparameter justification, preprocessing-sensitivity ablation, and abstention rate are universally relevant. Two-round review; round-2 reviewers fully satisfied.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Deep learning-based image analysis predicts PD-L1 status from H&E-stained histopathology images in breast cancer

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: 'This cohort consists of 652 recruited patients with ERBB2-positive metastatic breast cancer'. The authors assume that model validation on this cohort of patients remains valid despite the population consisting of only patients with ERBB2-positive, whereas the training data consists of all breast cancers. While this is perhaps a valid assumption, authors should address this in their analysis or discussion. For example, is there an association between ERBB2 positive and PDL1 positive in the validation set? Or between triple positive and PDL1 positive in the training set?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed per-subtype analysis on MA31 (including ERBB2+, Triple Negative, Luminal, IDC, ILC) showing the system generalized across all subtypes with AUC 0.81-0.92, supporting the validity of validation despite subtype mismatch.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Given the imbalance in the data, Precision-recall should be reported in parallel with ROC throughout.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not explicitly addressed in the visible response text; specificity and accuracy were added to Table 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: 'The calibration required held-out samples from MA31 that were then excluded from the final test and showed that indeed performance was increased (Figure 2b).' This was somewhat confusing? What is the value of calibration when the testing set is then reduced in size—won't reducing the size of the test set and essentially increasing the number of training images always lead to increased fit?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not visible in the extracted response pages; the issue concerns potential information leakage from calibration on test data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: What's the percentage of non-tumor or empty patches in training/validation/testing set? Were they removed for an unbiased evaluation in the validation/testing set?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained that no-tissue (19.6%) and no-tumor (3.6%) cases were excluded based on pathologist annotation BEFORE splitting into train/val/test, so the proportion of non-tumor/non-tissue patches was independent of the data split.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Moreover, in Figure 5b, the HE images look more blue in the predicted high-PS score group. it is unclear which information the model is utilizing; i.e., it is unclear whether the model looks at staining difference or tumor percentage or something else. Therefore, please utilize a deep learning interpretation method, such as GradCAM, to visualize which area the model is focusing on.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors provided GradCAM maps in the response letter but chose not to include in the paper because the maps were too coarse for cell-sized features; instead added additional statistical interpretability analyses.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The code does not seem to be made public, and the details of the architecture are not enough to allow anyone to re-code and re-produce it potentially. The methodology seems to be in line with recent publications done in the field of histopathology AI. However, the code has not been made available so no comment on reproducibility can be made. Any reason the authors do not make it available to the community?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added a Code Availability section with GitHub links and made the trained model publicly downloadable.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Histopathology WSI paper is OUT_OF_SCOPE per CLAUDE.md (imaging modality); however reviewers raised subtype-mismatch validity, calibration leakage, AUPRC-vs-ROC, interpretability and code-availability concerns directly informing MLGG. C03 (calibration on test set) is a particularly clean leakage-risk example. Resolution null where rebuttal didn't directly address the methodological objection.

proposed_updates.paper_title: Estimating diagnostic uncertainty in artificial intelligence assisted pathology using conformal prediction

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: My main concern is that for me that I find the statistical endpoints of the system hard to judge. In a diagnostic task, I am interested in positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) as well as sensitivity and specificity and F1 score (all of them at pre-specified thresholds). Can the authors provide these metrics obtained by their new system and compare them with SOTA? These pieces of information seem to be missing and should be reported in results, discussed in the discussion, and even mentioned in the abstract.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained conformal predictor framework uses validity/efficiency, but updated Table 2 with comparison of system performance with/without conformal prediction; updated abstract; added ROC curves with human pathologist combination (Fig S5). Noted PPV interpretation is complicated by training data oversampling.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A major point is that the source codes do not seem to be available. This is a must and the authors should provide a github link or even better, a DOI, to their codes.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors released conformal predictor code at https://github.com/heolss/Conformal_analyses and included a Code and Software Submission Checklist; underlying DL training code remains private due to internal infrastructure dependencies. PANDA challenge dataset publicly released.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Also, adherence to relevant reporting guidelines (TRIPOD, STARD, etc.) must be added.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors updated Statistical analysis section per TRIPOD and included a TRIPOD checklist with the revision.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The training data are from the same cohort. As a matter of fact, the corresponding author has published several papers using multi-center PCa cohorts. It will be more convincing if this study can expand to other large cohorts (including different human races) for both training and testing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added an external test set from Karolinska University Hospital (Test set 4) and additional external test set from Stavanger, Norway (n=1,220 slides).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The n number for the atypical prostate tissues is small. The authors are suggested to include a larger number of atypical prostate tissue slides or to include PCa variants such as neuroendocrine prostate cancer or prostate cancer with neuroendocrine differentiation to test the application of conformal prediction.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors extended atypical tissue test set by adding n=152 cases of benign mimics and rare subtypes; new Test set 5 now n=179, with conformal prediction flagging 80% of these as unusual cases.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The external data experiments should make it more clear if the model used was only trained on the single scanner (such as in the Figure 2 caption). It is consequently not clear if Figure 2 is showing evaluation of both models or just the single scanner model on all three test sets. Also, it would be helpful to see a similar analysis for a model trained on a dataset with both scanners, and also the reverse (training on Hamamatsu, evaluation on Aperio).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors updated Fig 2 caption to clarify single-scanner model, added reversed analysis (training on Hamamatsu, evaluation on Aperio) as Supplementary Figure S4 showing the conformal predictor identified systematic differences from training data in the new scanner.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Histopathology WSI paper is OUT_OF_SCOPE per CLAUDE.md (imaging modality); however reviewers raised excellent generalization, PPV/NPV reporting, TRIPOD compliance and code-availability concerns directly informing MLGG. Two-round review; round-2 reviewers mostly satisfied except for Reviewer #1 who still felt full training code should be public. Resolution of C02 marked null because the rebuttal partially addressed it (only conformal-predictor code, not training code).

proposed_updates.paper_title: Integrating deep learning CT-scan model, biological and clinical variables to predict severity of COVID-19 patients

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I have some serious reservations on the claims being made in this paper with regards to the superiority and CT scans being the 'strongest performance booster'. An increase of 0.02 and 0.03 in a test set of 150 and 137 patients cannot be considered significant (and they were not shown to be). Portability/robustness by testing an algorithm on a small subset of an already rather small number of patients from two hospitals that were already included in the training set cannot be claimed.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added thorough comparison with six different COVID risk scores (Fig. 3), and included statistical testing; trained a simpler ScanCov 6-variable score and showed it outperformed CALL, MIT analytics, Colombi, Yan scores. Authors acknowledged claim of CT-scan superiority needs softening.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although the revised manuscript shows in detail the comparison between previous models and the proposed ones, it still remains unclear which model, out of the Tri AI-segment, Tri AI-severity, and Tri RR is the final suggested model to use in each use-case. Authors should clearly explain whether they propose one, or all three models at different use-cases. Hence, unless the authors show a statistically significant difference of AUCs between C&B and any of the Tri models, the claims of superiority or improvement should be removed. The title should be rephrased, because it's not clear which part of 'clinical characteristics, lab tests and chest CTs' actually improve the model performance against which baseline model.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not visible in the round-2 extracted text.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How do you determine some hyper parameters when training the AI-segment and AI-severity models? In general, the data should be split into training set, validation set and testing set, while it seems that the validation set is omitted in the study.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified they used 5-fold cross-validation on the training set for hyperparameter selection, providing stronger evaluation than single train/val split.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To assess disease progression and build model to stratify risk, the authors measured the time from admission to critical severity, or death. However, there is no mention of when the CT was taken during the hospital course. Could you provide this information? Were all the chest CTs were obtained on admission? Failure to account for time-of-CT in the analysis could result in a lead time bias and data gathered at time of the clinical endpoints could skew the results for patients scanned earlier in the disease course.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified all CT scans were obtained within 48 hours following admission, now stated explicitly in the main text.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: One other point that was confusing is that their readings, although claimed to be prospective, were based on the consensus statement by STR, ACR, and RSNA. The consensus statement was made available online on March 25th. The authors claim that the reads happened prospectively, with the first patient being admitted on February 12th. I have trouble understanding whether these reads were indeed prospective or retrospective.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified the radiologist report template was available March 17, and reports were completed retrospectively for patients admitted before this date.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors used AUC to evaluate the performance of the classification model. The 95% confidence interval should be reported.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added 95% CIs to main text (already in supplementary Table 3).

new_fields._extraction_notes: CT imaging + clinical paper is OUT_OF_SCOPE per CLAUDE.md (imaging modality), but reviewers raised substantive methodology concerns including small-test-set significance, validation-set omission, time-of-scan lead-time bias, and prospective-vs-retrospective ambiguity that map directly to MLGG dimensions. Two reviewers, two rounds. Round-2 indicates outstanding concerns about marginal performance superiority and model-selection ambiguity were not fully resolved (resolution status null for those).

proposed_updates.paper_title: Real-time prediction of COVID-19 related mortality using electronic health records

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The patient cohorts/databases used should be better described in detail. E.g. how was the diagnosis Covid-19 made in these databases (SARS-CoV-2 PCR proven? diagnostic criteria?). Also include details on composition, quality of data used in manuscript, access etc.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified inclusion was based on positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR/RNA test, COVID-19 ICD codes, or both; reported that 6.31% of Optum diagnoses lacked a recorded positive test and noted CovEWS performance was robust in a later Optum Future cohort where all diagnoses had positive tests.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A major limitation is the fact that by far the most patients are included before treatment protocols were changed around the world to exclude antibiotics and include remdesivir, dexamethasone and anticoagulant therapy... It is thought that current overall mortality is less when compared to situations of a first wave/first responders in this pandemic. The authors address this in a limited fashion by having a secondary analysis in patients that presented in July. At the very least this should be highlighted in the limitation section.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors evaluated CovEWS on an Optum Future cohort recruited after RECOVERY trial results were reported and showed performance was sustained despite treatment changes; added reasoning for robustness to treatment-pattern changes (percentile-based risk score remains robust to absolute mortality probability shifts).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The paper describes the development, validation and performance of the CovEWS tool, but gives limited attention to the practical aspects and limitations of this tool... Could you elaborate on how you plan to introduce this tool into clinical practice and what specific steps are needed to prove the benefits of the tool?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion of two deployment options (standalone web app and EHR-integrated solution), and outlined future RCT to evaluate impact on resource use and outcomes.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Could you elaborate on why you chose to present the mortality risk in a 0-100 percentile range? This reviewer believes that it would be hard to translate such a number into a clinical action. An absolute mortality risk could be much clearer.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained that percentile-based score avoids misleading direct probability interpretation, is robust across prediction horizons, and is stable under shifts in absolute mortality due to treatment changes.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the results section, an excellent overview of the performance of the CovEWS in relation to other predictors of mortality is given in figure 1. However, the comparison with the SOFA score has some limitations. The SOFA score is based on an intensive care population and should thus do much better in patient A than in patient B. This reviewer feels that a comparison with the MEWS would be more insightful. The limitation of the SOFA score should at least be acknowledged in this regard.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added MEWS (Modified Early Warning Score) as an additional comparator in Figures 1 and 3 and supplementary tables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It was unclear how to make fair comparisons when there exist a huge number of missing variables. For instance, there are more than 99% values of hs-CRP (one of key variables in [17]) missing in the external validation dataset. ... CovEWS demanded high dimensional inputs for mortality prediction... It is expected that the prediction accuracy will drop significantly if a large number of factors are missing.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified MICE estimators were derived from the training set only (Optum) and applied to other folds/datasets; noted hs-CRP can be accurately imputed from highly-correlated CRP; argued evaluation under realistic missingness is fairer than complete-case analysis.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: TriNetX dataset was selected for the external validation in this study. A significant concern about this study is the generalizability. The model performance on this external dataset seems not optimal (even the author explained the missing value problem). Especially, results in the time-varying plot in Figure 3 show that only about 50% of the identified high-risk patients (CovEWS score is 90-100 indicating a very high mortality risk) eventually died. The authors should consider if TriNex is an appropriate dataset for generalizability analysis and explicitly discuss the impact of missing variables.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors defended TriNetX as appropriate precisely because it tests robustness across geography, population and missingness; noted CovEWS still significantly outperformed all other scoring systems on TriNetX.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Baseline methods from Yan et al. and Liang et al. show promising results in their studies. However, these studies were done at the initial breakout of COVID-19 with fewer patient samples and most of the patients were Asian. Without re-training or re-tuning these models with datasets used in this study, it is unfair to say the model proposed in this study is superior to these methods.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors argued it is appropriate to independently evaluate published models on a larger more representative cohort precisely because original cohorts were small and non-representative; noted none of the compared methods including CovEWS were retrained on the external TriNetX cohort.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: When splitting the dataset, the authors wrote: 'To demonstrate the generalizability of predictions made by CovEWS, we limited the training of CovEWS to a training cohort of 14 215 (30%) patients from the Optum cohort, used 9 477 (20%) Optum patients for model selection, and evaluated CovEWS against both a held-out test cohort of 14 215 (30%) patients from the Optum cohort.' What about the rest 20% patients?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the percentage error; clarified that training cohort actually corresponded to 23,692 patients (50%) and corrected the manuscript.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The CovEWS model itself is not interpretable since the authors applied neural networks to enhance feature learning ability of the model. To address this issue, the developed CovEWS model identified clinically-relevant factors for mortality prediction using the Integrated Gradient method (IG). Importance of different factors can be ranked based on the scores produced by IG. However, it seems that this approach cannot provide detailed threshold for these factors in order to set up clinical warning in practice.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors explained warnings should be set on patient-level CovEWS score thresholds rather than per-feature thresholds; pointed to the manuscript's threshold section (S.10).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The use of ICD-9/10 codes as a predictor is not clinically useful. Physicians never code their diagnosis - most of diagnoses are coded after admission or discharge. How does the clinician use the model?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors stated that diagnostic codes are only used from the time they were entered into the EHR (i.e., predictive performance reflects real-world coding timing); reported that 85.0% (TriNetX) and 72.5% (Optum) of diagnoses were coded and available before patient inclusion based on COVID-19 diagnosis/test.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The definition of outcome (death) is not validated. In addition to the non-validated study population (i.e. COVID-19 diagnosis), the uncertainty in death may bias the results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors noted mortality outcomes were validated at source by healthcare organizations; acknowledged systematic bias from outpatient deaths possibly being missed; added limitation about incomplete outpatient death records.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The lack of prospective evaluation limits the generalizability/transportability. In general, the lack of generalizability/transportability is more problematic when using claims data.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors pointed to evaluation on the TriNetX cohort (5,005 patients, 24 HCOs, international) and a temporally-separated Optum Future cohort; argued these demonstrate generalization to new environments and conditions.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I was not convinced by the performance and comparison results using datasets that has more than 99.28% missing measurements for one of the key variables used in different models. In other words, there is only 1 in every 140 patients that has a measurement. How can one infer/estimate the measurements of other patients based on this single measurement? ... MICE is good for imputing missing values... But there is a more fundamental problem before applying MICE: what is the largest percentage that MICE can impute with a trustable performance? When the ratio of missing values exceeds this threshold, the imputed values become random guess. Then the conclusion drawn could be wrong!
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified the 99.28% missingness is in the external TriNetX test set; the MICE estimator was learned on training set (Optum, 96.62% missingness in hsCRP, but still ~800 patients available); argued that percentage missingness is not the relevant threshold and that imputation quality depends on cross-covariate associations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: My previous concerns on the fairness of comparison using largely missing datasets still hold. There are too many missing values for variables in ALL compared models. Using, for instance, values of CRP to estimate those of hs-CRP is not a good idea. Not only they have different means, they have different impact (Table S4). One shall notice that the p-values were calculated using chi-squared tests are different (0.52 versus < 0.005).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors enumerated 4 evaluation options (impute on all, withhold predictions, complete-case only, no comparison) and defended their chosen approach; added 6 sub-cohort analyses with fewer missing covariates showing rankings sustained.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Three reviewers, three rounds (round 1, round 2 R2 mostly unsatisfied + R3 satisfied + R1 satisfied; round 3 R2 satisfied). Strong methodological focus throughout, especially on missingness, MICE validity, and external validation under distribution shift. C06/C07/C14/C15 are the same thread (Reviewer #2's persistent missingness concern across rounds) — kept separate to track resolution dynamics. Missingness thread never formally resolved by reviewer in round 3 text — reviewer simply moves on. Author response style is rebuttal-heavy with frequent disagreement.

proposed_updates.paper_title: A machine learning model for identifying patients at risk for wild-type transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: ICD coding for wild-type amyloid was used as the gold standard - this is flawed as we do not know what the specific ECG, imaging, and histology findings are for these patients, or what criteria was used to make this diagnosis. Even within wild-type amyloid there are many different genetic variants all with different phenotypes, and the authors fail to tease this out as their ICD coding was purely 'wild-type'. ... Similarly, 'heart failure' is very broad term and is often miscoded. Further, it is HFPEF that we are interested in, and not just any heart failure.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors disagreed that wild-type ATTR has genetic variants (by definition it is diagnosed in absence of TTR variants); disagreed that only HFpEF is relevant (citing ATTR-ACT data showing 22% HFrEF, 29% HFmrEF, 50% HFpEF); acknowledged HF code limitation in discussion text.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: NRI and IDI was calculated and at least one should be included in the results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added IDI=0.039 (95% CI 0.031-0.048) p<0.00001 and category-less NRI=0.25 (95% CI 0.22-0.28) p<0.00001 to results, indicating ML algorithm improved over conventional predictors.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The biggest concern is that that a sizable number of the controls may have undiagnosed amyloidosis. The authors mention it as a limitation in the 'limitations' paragraph, but that is not sufficient. They should address it in the results/discussion and discuss how using models with higher specificity in this instance may be inferior to those with higher sensitivity.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion noting future prospective studies with systematic application of gold standard tests will be needed for further development and validation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the model described page 10, how did they deal with the differential use of BNP and NT-proBNP and differential use of troponin I, troponin T, and hs-troponin T? Definition of high is different in Text and in Table 5 legend (0.4 in former and 0.04 in latter). The latter is correct for abnormal whereas the former is not.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified Northwestern uses a single assay (BNP not NTproBNP, troponin I not troponin T) so assays were uniform; corrected troponin threshold typo to >0.04 ng/ml.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The obvious point - the model performance is predicated upon assignment of cases and controls. We can presume for the sake of argument that cases of ATTRwt-CM are likely to be accurate. But similar to the point made in the discussion regarding the NW dataset, there definitively unrecognized cases of ATTRwt-CM in the control cohort. ... ideally the negative controls should come from a cohort who have all undergone PYP scintigraphy (which all but excludes cardiac ATTR amyloidosis). Given that this undoubtedly compromises the assessment of accuracy of the algorithm, the editors may wish to consider requesting the addition of a more fully characterised control cohort.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged the limitation; stated they are not aware of large-scale cohorts of HF patients consecutively examined with confirmatory PYP scintigraphy; framed the algorithm as a starting point to stimulate such studies.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The responses to reviewer #4 are acceptable. I do strongly encourage to not perpetuate the use of AUROC as a metric in such situations and instead focus on AUPRC values, the increase in post-test PPV etc. It does us all a disservice to play up AUROC, and numbers in the 80s, when they are practically useless in the use case envisioned and for low prevalence events can misguide a lot of readers.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors removed AUROC listings from the abstract; opted to keep AUROC in body with positive/negative likelihood ratios (Table 5) rather than adding AUPRC (citing clinician interpretability concerns).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: However that increased case finding ability needs to be balanced with the harm that will be inflicted on the false positives. Will they be tested with a 'confirmatory test'? How much does that cost, is it invasive? And net-net what is the number needed to test (and $$ needed to spend) to find one new case of ATTR-CM, which we are currently missing. That kind of discussion is essential.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added discussion of downstream confirmatory testing pathway (light-chain blood/urine tests, PYP scintigraphy, endomyocardial biopsy, TTR genetic testing) and noted formal cost-effectiveness analysis is outside scope but warranted.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Authors have made a valiant effort to address the limitations cited by the previous reviewers. There is indeed value to this paper in potentially screening the population for Wild-type TTR Amyloidosis, however, I do agree with previous reviewers' suggestions that 'the algorithm only flags individuals potentially at-risk for wild-type ATTR-CM but does not diagnose the condition'. This is not forthcoming and the manuscript title and results may mislead a reader. ... I would tone down all throughout the manuscript carefully any claims towards diagnosis and early detection of ATTRwt-CM.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors changed title to 'A Machine Learning Model of Medical Claims Data for Identifying Patients at Risk for Wild-Type Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy'; revised discussion to emphasize 'targeted testing and confirmation' rather than 'diagnosis and early detection'.

new_fields._extraction_notes: Editorial note: manuscript was previously reviewed at another journal (so reviewers #2,#5,#6,#7 are inherited from prior submission); subsequent round at Nature Comms added reviewers #7,#8,#9. Five distinct reviewers (#2,#5,#6,#7,#9) provided substantive comments in this PDF. Two rounds at Nature Communications. Dominant theme: case/control label fidelity given ICD-only ascertainment (C01, C03, C05) - flagged CRITICAL because the model is trained against a non-validated outcome. Reviewer #7's AUROC critique for low-prevalence events maps cleanly to MLGG-E02.

proposed_updates.paper_title: The T cell receptor repertoire of tumor infiltrating T cells is predictive and prognostic for cancer survival

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors studied 16 patients with metastatic melanoma. At first glance, the sample size appears exceedingly small and if this association (OS and high TCR clonality) is true, it should be broadened to be truly representative of newly diagnosed patients to convince one that others can build upon these results. The limited information in the data summary is inadequate.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added more detailed clinical characteristics in Table 1 and analysed 3 additional independent cohorts (Tumeh 2014, Roh 2017, Amaria 2019) in new Figure 1e-j, confirming that high TIL/Tc clonality in pre-treatment biopsies correlated with benefit from therapy.
